articles.title: 4 soldiers from El Salvador missing in Haiti after attack by gangs
articles.summary: Gangs in Haiti opened fire on an armoured vehicle over the weekend, leaving four soldiers from El Salvador unaccounted for in the first major attack since an international gang suppression force…

image.caption: Armoured vehicles that are part of the gang suppression force in Haiti are seen on patrol in the Tabarre neighbourhood in Port-au-Prince on Monday. (Odelyn Joseph/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

Gangs in Haiti opened fire on an armoured vehicle over the weekend, leaving four soldiers from El Salvador unaccounted for in the first major attack since an international gang suppression force began operations in the violence-wracked Caribbean country.
Soldiers believed to have fled burning vehicle, but are since accounted for
The attack occurred Sunday in Croix-des-Bouquets, a once-peaceful community in Haiti's capital, Port-au-Prince, that is now controlled by violent gangs.
The armed forces of El Salvador said in a statement Monday that the four aviation technicians were returning to camp when their armoured vehicle was attacked with explosives and set on fire.
The military noted that the four men managed to flee the burning vehicle and it is working with international forces to "establish contact and determine the location of our military personnel."
Salvadoran authorities said that helicopters were dispatched to the area but they, too, came under fire as they dispersed armed men in the area.

items: UN Security Council extends mandate of anti-gang force in Haiti into 2027
At least 47 people killed in violent weekend attacks in Haiti, UN says

blocks.text: "Multiple attempts to approach by land and air have been made, but these have been hampered by the intensity of the fighting," the Salvadoran military said.

The weapons and ammunition gangs are using are not made in Haiti and will continue to find ways to enter the country, Wien-Weibert Arthus, Haiti's deputy permanent representative to the UN, told the UN Security Council Monday.
"This latest episode is a reminder, as if we really needed one, of the fact that the security challenges in Haiti are complex and complicated," he said.
"We hope that those who are missing will be able to go back to their families unscathed."

Gang violence has displaced nearly 1.5 million people, a record, across Haiti in recent years, with more than 5,700 people killed or injured from January to mid-September, and more than 230 others kidnapped, according to the UN.
Warning from Waltz
Mike Waltz, the U.S. ambassador to the UN, condemned the attack during the UN Security Council meeting on Haiti.
"We believe the four men survived, but they do remain unaccounted for," he said. "We will bring you home."
UN chief visits Haiti as new Gang Suppression Force moves in
Waltz said that gangs attacked the armoured vehicle with "hundreds of bullets and explosives."
"To the gangs and gang leaders who carried out this cowardly attack, if you think you're going to intimidate this coalition into retreat, you have made a terrible mistake," he said.
The gang suppression force said in a statement that it's assessing the situation and has advised residents where the attack occurred to remain indoors.
"Gangs are testing the gang suppression force," Jack Christofides, the force's special representative, said at the UN Monday as he noted that attacks against the force have recently increased.

He warned that gangs have carried out reprisal killings in some areas following operations by Haitian and international forces, and that they have pushed deeper into places including the community of Kenscoff and the Artibonite region.
"The reality is that we cannot be everywhere at once," Christofides said.
Haiti prepares for an election
The area where the armoured vehicle was targeted is controlled by gangs including Chèn Méchan, Kraze Barye and 400 Mawozo.
A gang suppression force armoued vehicle is seen patrolling in the Tabarre neighbourhood of Port-au-Prince on Monday. (Odelyn Joseph/The Associated Press)

Romain Le Cour, head of the Haiti Observatory at the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, said that while some gangs have been under pressure since the suppression force was deployed, "others want to show that they can strike back."
"If these soldiers are indeed being held, the groups gain (an) edge to negotiate and to pressure the security forces," he said.

In September 2025, the UN Security Council authorized the 5,550-member force to replace a former Kenya-led multinational force that struggled with a lack of funds and resources as it tried to help Haiti's National Police quell gang violence.

items: Hundreds flee homes in Haiti amid new wave of gang violence
Doctors Without Borders forced to evacuate hospital in Haiti's capital as gang violence ramps up

blocks.text: The gang suppression force has more than 2,000 troops on the ground in Haiti, including soldiers from Chad, Jamaica and Guatemala.
"The force is making a difference with what it has," Christofides said, adding that authorities have started to see early signs of reduced gang influence and control in certain areas.

No one has claimed responsibility for the attack on the Salvadoran troops. It comes as Haiti prepares for its first general election in more than a decade and showcases the power of the gangs that control an estimated 70 per cent of Port-au-Prince.
Carlos Ruiz Massieu, the UN special envoy to Haiti, said at Monday's meeting that electoral preparations "have reached an unprecedented level of progress."

He said that more than 35 parties and political groups have registered, along with 3,500 candidates. Among them is former Haitian president Michel Martelly, who was sanctioned in November 2022 by Canada and in August 2024 by the U.S., which accused him of facilitating drug trafficking and sponsoring multiple gangs.

articles.title: Anthropic sued by major Canadian news publishers for copyright claims in Ontario court
articles.summary: In the lawsuit filed on Oct. 6, Postmedia, Torstar, The Globe and Mail and The Canadian Press say Anthropic infringed on their copyright by using their content to develop its large language AI model,…

image.caption: Pages from the Anthropic website displayed earlier this year. Multiple major Canadian news outlets are suing the AI company, saying Anthropic infringed on their copyright by using their content to train its large language model. (Patrick Sison/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Business

In the lawsuit filed on Oct. 6, Postmedia, Torstar, The Globe and Mail and The Canadian Press say Anthropic infringed on their copyright by using their content to develop its large language AI model, Claude.
Newspapers say Anthropic infringed on their copyright by using their content to develop AI model Claude
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Oct 19, 2026 3:44 PM EDT | Last Updated: 1 hour ago
A coalition of news publishers that includes Canada's largest newspapers is suing the AI company Anthropic in an Ontario court.
Postmedia, Torstar, The Globe and Mail and The Canadian Press say Anthropic infringed on their copyright by using their content to develop its large language AI model, Claude.

"Anthropic has capitalized on the commercial success of its AI models, building an expansive suite of services, and raised significant capital — all without obtaining a valid licence from any of the News Media Companies," says the statement of claim.
"In doing so, Anthropic has been substantially and unjustly enriched to the detriment of the News Media Companies."
The lawsuit, filed on Oct. 6, was first reported by the news site Cartt.ca. Anthropic has not responded to a request for comment. The allegations have not been proven in court.

items: Ottawa weighs plans on AI, copyright as OpenAI fights Ontario court jurisdiction

blocks.text: The statement of claim says Anthropic breached the news media websites' terms of service and circumvented technological protection measures they put in place to restrict copying of their content.

The claim says the news outlets "are responsible for generating a significant portion of Canada's journalistic content — from daily print broadsheets to round-the-clock digital news coverage," and collectively have millions of readers.

"To obtain content for ingestion into its models and services, Anthropic deliberately 'scrapes' (i.e. accesses and copies) enormous amounts of text data from the internet and from the Plaintiffs' Websites," the claim says.

The news outlets say Anthropic then uses that content, without authorization or consent, to develop its AI models. It says Anthropic also scrapes content on an ongoing basis in response to user prompts.
Canadian news organizations, including CBC, sue ChatGPT creator

"Notwithstanding concerns raised by several content creators across various industries, including through numerous other lawsuits and public criticism, Anthropic has done nothing to curtail its unlawful behaviour," the statement of claim says.
The same companies also launched, alongside CBC/Radio-Canada, a lawsuit against OpenAI in 2024. That case has yet to be settled.

News publishers abroad have also sued tech companies for using their articles to train AI systems. The New York Times sued OpenAI for its use of the paper's copyrighted material, and the Justice Department sided with the tech company last month.

blocks.text: What we know so far
First of all let’s set out what we know so far about what happened in Wangaratta yesterday.

items: Helen Haines has been critically injured in an alleged attack involving a car outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, regional Victoria, at about 3.35pm on Monday.
The independent MP was taken to Melbourne’s Alfred hospital and underwent surgery overnight. She remains in a critical condition.

A 43-year-old man from Tarrawingee is in custody, and the alleged attack is being investigated by the Australian federal police, Asio and the joint counter-terror taskforce. The motive is not yet known. A knife was allegedly found in his car after he was detained by a passerby when he got out of his vehicle.

Anthony Albanese, Angus Taylor, the Greens leader, David Shoebridge, the One Nation leader, Pauline Hanson, and politicians across the parliament have sent their thoughts and well wishes to Haines and her family.
In a press conference on Monday evening, Albanese described Haines, who has represented Indi since 2019, as a “thoroughly decent human being, full of integrity and respected right across parliament”.

Addressing the media in Wangaratta on Monday evening, acting supt Ashley Mason said police were still investigating whether the incident was targeted. He said there was no ongoing threat to the community and nothing to indicate the parties were known to each other.

The United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) says ‌funding shortages are forcing major cuts to its aid program in Gaza, leaving about 500,000 people without monthly food support in a territory where two-thirds of the population struggle to get enough to eat.
Funding shortages mean 500,000 people have no food supports as other meal programs and food rations are cut

The United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) says ‌funding shortages are forcing major cuts to its aid program in Gaza, leaving about 500,000 people without monthly food support in a territory where two-thirds of the population already struggle to get enough to eat.
The WFP said it was reducing the number of recipients of its monthly assistance to 1.1 million ​people from 1.6 million.

In addition, food rations have been halved, cash ​assistance has been cut for 75,000 families, and the number of daily hot meals for those unable to cook has fallen from 250,000 to to 150,000, with some families in hard-to-reach areas now ​receiving a hot meal only every other day.

items: Bearing Witness: Canadian Doctors in Gaza
Gaza is slowly moving beyond survival mode — 3 years after the war began

blocks.text: The WFP said about 1.4 million people, or ⁠two-thirds of Gaza's population, face crisis ⁠levels of food insecurity or worse, including roughly 200,000 ‌people in emergency conditions.

Last year's U.S.-brokered Gaza ceasefire calls for the eventual reconstruction of the territory. But little progress has been made toward implementing the deal to end the conflict that includes terms for Hamas to disarm and Israel to withdraw its troops.

Carl Skau, acting executive director of the World Food Programme (WFP), centre, visits a soup kitchen in Gaza Sunday. The program is being forced to slash aid to the territory due to funding cuts. (Mahmoud Issa/Reuters)
Life still 'brutal' in Gaza

"It's a year into the agreement of this ceasefire. Well, life is still brutal here. There is no proper shelter … no basic services. There is no safety, no security," Carl Skau, the acting executive director of the WFP, told Reuters in ‌Gaza.
"These cuts are happening just as we are facing the fourth winter," he said. "I've been through the winters here, absolutely brutal."
The WFP said it urgently needs $450 million US over the next six months to maintain critical operations in Gaza and the Israeli-occupied West Bank.

items: Israelis mourn on 3rd anniversary of Oct. 7 attacks as Palestinians grapple with war it sparked
Israeli strikes kill 5, including 4 women, in Gaza, health officials say

blocks.text: "We tell the world now is not ​the time to look away. This is the time to step up to sustain this support, to protect the progress that has been made, but also to ⁠push for early recovery," said Skau.

Israeli forces still hold more than 60 per cent of the territory and conduct almost daily airstrikes, ⁠while Hamas controls much of the area where more than two million Palestinians live, mostly in temporary shelters with ⁠what ⁠aid agencies call inadequate aid supplies.
Life is brutal inside Gaza, one year into the ceasefire

The Hamas-run Gaza ​government media office described the WFP announcement as "catastrophic" and said it might accelerate famine in the enclave, calling for more funding ​to aid agencies to prevent it.

"On ⁠top of the circumstances and the difficult life, you want to make it even harder on us," said Palestinian Sabrine Kuhail, standing by a tent shelter at a displacement site in Nuseirat refugee camp in central Gaza Strip.
"You made us hungry for three years with war, destruction, siege and the bloodshed that is not stopping. What do you want from us? Enough, enough, ⁠we are tired."

articles.title: 'You Can See Everything' sells out theatres, and people can't stop talking about it
articles.summary: 'You Can See Everything' is the movie everyone wants to talk about but no one wants spoiled. It's drawing big numbers at the box office.

image.caption: Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes appears in a still from the documentary You Can See Everything. (A24)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New
'You Can See Everything' is the movie everyone wants to talk about but no one wants spoiled. It's drawing big numbers at the box office.
'An absolutely phenomenal crazy fever dream'
You Can See Everything is the movie everyone wants to talk about but no one wants spoiled.
Maybe that's why so many people rushed to theatres on opening weekend to see the nearly three-hour documentary about Theranos founder and convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes.

Whatever the reason, the film made more than $15 million US in ticket sales during its debut weekend — the second-largest opening weekend for a non-musical documentary in domestic box office history, behind only 2004's Fahrenheit 9/11.
It's a considerable achievement, considering You Can See Everything had a limited release at just 855 theatres in Canada and the U.S.

The reviews following its debut were overwhelmingly positive: rated 99 per cent fresh on Rotten Tomatoes, and scoring a 4.8 on Letterboxd, making it the highest-rated movie in the site's history. (Both those ratings have come down since then, but only slightly.)
As the five-star reviews started pouring in online, so too did the comments: "My mouth was agape for basically the entire last two hours," from Letterboxd user James (Schaffrillas).
"Just an absolutely phenomenal crazy fever dream of a documentary," said user vgoodatkissing.
You can read everything — no spoilers here

The documentary's premise is straightforward. A film crew, including dual director-producers Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, briefly move in with Holmes, her partner Billy Evans and their children, and document their lives, 34 days before she is due to start serving an extended prison sentence for fraud.
Toronto film critic Teri Hart says watching You Can See Everything in theatres was a visceral experience.
"People were actually physically leaning into the screen," she told CBC News. "There were gasps at times; people applauded at the end of the movie, lots of laughter."

"You leave this movie and you don't know if you want to talk about Nathan Fielder, if you want to talk about Elizabeth Holmes, if you want to talk about Billy or if you want to talk 'where did they put the camera.'"

items: Nathan Fielder's You Can See Everything gazes into the abyss of Elizabeth Holmes

blocks.text: The trailer gives audiences a glimpse into Fielder and Holmes's unusual dynamic.

"Nathan Fielder is not afraid of awkward. Nathan Fielder is not afraid of asking questions in a way that is unlike anybody else," said Hart. "He has a level of provocateur, I think, that is so fascinating to watch.
Boundary-pushing directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim documented Elizabeth Holmes's life during the 34 days before she was sent to prison for defrauding investors. (A24)
"Place him with Elizabeth Holmes, who also has a unique way of communicating, and you have magic."

Indeed, the documentary delivers on the intense and deliberately uncomfortable interviews that Fielder, a Canadian who was born in Vancouver, became known for on shows like Nathan for You, as well as his paradigm-shifting approach to the truth.
Hart calls the documentary a theatrical experience few people will have ever had — one that may lead audiences to question what we think of as the truth.
Another win for A24

You Can See Everything was distributed and partly produced by A24, the same company behind some of this year's most talked-about films, including Olivia Wilde's The Invite, the Anthony Bourdain biopic Tony and the record-breaking horror Backrooms.

"A24 is a distributor that has a brand. And that brand is — to my mind — working with auteurs, working with writer-directors or even just directors that really have a specific vision and have a strong, strong artistry associated with them," said Hart.
Nathan Fielder searches for truth in You Can See Everything

items: Tony director says making biopic was like being in 'a conspiracy with Anthony Bourdain

blocks.text: She said that's helped A24 make a splash, as the company pushes back against the general consensus that Hollywood has no new ideas.
As a movie lover, Hart said she is grateful for anything that gets people back in the theatres and talking about what they've seen. She says You Can See Everything is a great example of that.

"They're, like, shocked and surprised or walking out of the theater with all kinds of thoughts and ideas and questions. Because let's be clear, this movie does not tie anything up with a nice pretty bow. It does not. So people have questions.
"And I think that that is a really thrilling experience for people to share with strangers. "
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Helen Surgenor is a producer for CBC News based in Toronto, currently working for the entertainment unit. She spent years waking up before dawn to make the daily news podcast World Report. She has reported in Alberta, Iqaluit and Barbados. You can reach her at helen.surgenor@cbc.ca.

articles.title: N.L. man sentenced to 7 years in prison for shooting snowmobiler in head
articles.summary: A Port au Port West man has been sentenced to seven years in prison for shooting a snowmobiler in the head almost two years ago.

image.caption: Harold Wayne Hynes, who is at the Bishop’s Falls Correctional Centre, appeared before court by teleconference on Monday. (Colleen Connors/CBC)

blocks.text: Nfld. & Labrador·New
A Port au Port West man has been sentenced to seven years in prison for shooting a snowmobiler in the head almost two years ago.
Harold Wayne Hynes pleaded guilty of aggravated assault and careless use of a firearm
A Port au Port West man has been sentenced to seven years in prison for shooting a snowmobiler in the head almost two years ago on Newfoundland's west coast.
Justice Trina Simms sentenced Harold Wayne Hynes, 68, over Zoom from a Corner Brook courtroom late Monday afternoon over the shooting of Chad Hickey on Feb. 21, 2025.

“Obviously no sentence is justice enough for what Chad and our family has gone through in the last 20 months, but I am very happy that Justice Simms chose the maximum sentence the Crown presented," said Alex Hickey, Chad Hickey’s wife, who was in the courtroom Monday.
Hynes was arrested and charged with attempted murder, careless use of a firearm and aggravated assault on March 16, 2025.
Justice Simms noted the nature of the act itself — firing a shotgun — endangered Chad Hickey but also put the community in danger.

The incident happened on Gravel's Pond, a small saltwater pond near Hynes' home where Hickey and his friend were crossing on a snowmobile. Hynes fired his shotgun from a window in his home, hitting Hickey in the head.
Hickey, who wasn't wearing a helmet at the time, suffered a brain injury and underwent surgery to remove bullet fragments from his head. He permanently lost the use of parts of his left side.
He spent 33 days in the hospital, followed by six weeks at the Miller Centre in St. John's for rehabilitation, where he had to re-learn how to dress himself and tie his shoes.
During that time, his now-wife Alex had their first child. She got emotional when Hynes' sentence was read aloud in the courtroom.
"It was a really difficult time, me being eight months pregnant, for our family, our whole community." Alex Hickey said.
Alex Hickey says she's happy with the sentence Harold Wayne Hynes received but their family still lives with the impact of the shooting. (Colleen Connors/CBC)

Initially, Hynes pleaded not guilty to all charges but on July 20, he changed his plea to guilty of aggravated assault and careless use of a firearm. The attempted murder charge was discharged and there was no trial.
Chad Hickey told the court during the August sentencing hearing that his injuries robbed him of the opportunities to be a first-time father and he will never get that back.

“It was really really hard at first. He wasn't able to pick up his own child, buckle him into the car seat or feed him a bottle. But thank God he is doing much much better and we are now able to live our new normal," said Alex Hickey.
Chad Hickey was not in the courtroom Monday because he was working, captaining a fishing boat.
He does have balancing issues and only one functioning hand, which prevents him from doing a lot of physical labour, but he does have accommodations on board.
“He puts on a brave face," said Alex Hickey. “He is back fishing which is his passion. Just because it seems that he is living a normal life, doesn't mean it comes without challenges."

Hynes was not in the courtroom either. He appeared by teleconference from the Bishop’s Falls Correctional Centre. Hynes didn't show much emotion during his sentencing, appearing calm and looking at the screen.

Hynes lived in Port au Port West but spent most of his life working away as a millwright. He moved back in 2019 and he has no family. He sufferes from chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, which has gotten worse since he was incarcerated.
He did apologize to the family during the sentencing hearing, but Alex Hickey says it means nothing.
“I don't take it. He knows what he did. He knows what he did when he pulled the trigger. There are no words that could take that back, unfortunately," she said.
Hynes faces a lifetime prohibition on using a firearm and he is not to have any communication with Hickey or his immediate family members.
Alex and Chad celebrated their wedding a month ago. Their son is now 18-months-old.

articles.title: Protesters unveil melting Ron DeSantis statue to signify his inaction on climate crisis
articles.summary:
Florida governor has consistently opposed any legislation to curb planet-heating emissions, calling it a ‘radical climate agenda’

A life-sized statue of Ron DeSantis, the Florida governor,…

blocks.text: A life-sized statue of Ron DeSantis, the Florida governor, was unveiled and promptly began melting in front of an audience in Tallahassee in a symbolic protest at his rejection of action on the climate crisis.

The silvery statue, revealed to an audience of onlookers last week, melted away to show a skull under DeSantis’s face. The structure was cast from solid gallium, a metal that melts at 85.6F (29.8C), which is below summertime high temperatures frequently reached in Tallahassee, Florida’s capital.
The environmentalists behind the statue-based protest said it was a fitting monument to DeSantis’s eight years as Florida governor, which comes to an end in January.

blocks.caption: The face of the statue melted away to reveal a skull-like structure under it. Photograph: 350 Action

blocks.text: The Republican has frequently criticized what he has called a “radical climate agenda”, blocking the ability of Florida municipalities to slash planet-heating pollution and even erased terms such as “climate change” and “greenhouse gas emissions” from Florida state law.

This law has hindered the ability of state agencies to even mention a climate crisis that poses an outsized threat to Florida. In classrooms, meanwhile, state education regulations are also ensuring the steady elimination of any reference to climate change.
“I am not a global warming person, I don’t want that label on me,” DeSantis, who unsuccessfully ran to become Republican nominee for US president in 2024, said in 2018.

Southern Florida is acutely threatened by sea level rise, while homes and businesses across the entire state have been increasingly lashed by powerful hurricanes, worsened by rising global temperatures. The increasing damage wrought by storms supercharged by ocean and atmospheric heat has proved so costly that several major insurers have exited Florida entirely.

The state’s stance towards the climate crisis looks unlikely to change, however. Florida has become a Republican bastion in recent years and Byron Donalds, the GOP candidate, is heavily favored to win the governor’s race in next month’s midterm elections.

blocks.caption: The installation, called ‘DENIAL,’ was created by Uncommon, an advertising agency, climate advocacy group 350 Action and M ss ng P eces, a production company. Photograph: 350 Action

blocks.text: Donalds has said he wants to maintain Florida’s environment but has said he doesn’t accept the link between climate change and human actions, despite scientific consensus that the burning of fossil fuels is causing temperatures to rise.

“The climate crisis is one of the top issues facing our planet today. And yet, some candidates running for office still deny it’s happening, and deny the bold climate action that the people want.” said Candice Fortin, campaign manager at 350Action, the environmental group behind the DeSantis statue, along with advertising agency Uncommon.

“That’s why it’s more important than ever to deny them back at the ballot box,” Fortin added. “If everyone who cares about people and our planet makes their voices heard on election cay, we’ll be too loud to deny.”

DeSantis has defended his position on climate. “We’re restoring sanity in our approach to energy and rejecting the agenda of the radical green zealots,” DeSantis said in a post on the X social media platform when making climate a lower state priority in May 2024.

articles.title: Over three dozen Congress members’ offices targeted with white powder envelopes
articles.summary:
Envelopes containing powder come weeks before midterms as federal agents try to identify who is behind campaign

More than three dozen members of US Congress have had their offices targeted…

blocks.text: More than three dozen members of US Congress have had their offices targeted with envelopes containing white powder, less than three weeks before the 3 November midterms, as federal agents try to identify who is behind the campaign.

The latest is the Virginia Democrat Suhas Subramanyam, whose Leesburg district office was evacuated on Monday after an envelope containing a suspicious substance arrived. He said the office was cleared quickly, adding that “acts of political intimidation have no place in our country”.
Subramanyam’s office said preliminary tests showed the powder was not hazardous.

Law enforcement sources told ABC News that more than 100 letters thought to contain white powder are circulating in the US mail system. The FBI, Capitol police and US Postal Inspection Service are investigating, according to a notice sent to Senate staff on Thursday.

Election offices in at least 15 states had reported receiving or being targeted by suspicious mail by Thursday evening, according to the Tampa Free Press, which cited federal authorities. No suspect has been named, and federal authorities have not released a confirmed figure.
The FBI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Senators have been targeted across the political spectrum, and country. Letters addressed to the Democratic Senate minority leader, Chuck Schumer, and California senator Alex Padilla were intercepted by authorities, while Chris Murphy of Connecticut said the FBI, the Senate sergeant at arms and Capitol police alerted his team of a letter as well. Republicans in South Dakota, Texas and Nebraska were also targeted, with Mike Rounds saying his Sioux Falls office was evacuated, along with Pete Ricketts and Ted Cruz also reporting a suspicious letter.

In the House, at least 10 people were exposed after white powder was sent to the offices of the New York Democrats Hakeem Jeffries, Ritchie Torres and Tom Suozzi. In California, Jimmy Panetta said a staffer opened an envelope at his Santa Cruz office, then cleared the room and called 911. He said such attempts to intimidate “will not deter us from doing our job”. In Massachusetts, five staffers left Seth Moulton’s Salem office while police investigated, and testing found no substances of concern.
Investigators have described several common features connecting the suspicious letters sent to public officials and election centers.

The FBI has stated that the recovered envelopes were processed through a north Texas mail processing center and carry a postmark or stamp reading “Thinking of You”. Senate staff and House offices were warned to watch for plain white envelopes featuring these distinct markings.
The vast majority of these envelopes were intercepted by the US Postal Inspection Service and screening facilities before being delivered.
In 2024, election officials were targeted in 17 states before the 2024 presidential election, and no suspect has been named in this case.

articles.title: ‘Crucial opportunity to act’ as study finds most of Europe’s wild bee species in decline
articles.summary:
As Cop17 kicks off, records since 1921 show more bee species declining than increasing in all parts of Europe except the Alps

Most of Europe’s wild bee species and about half of its hover…

blocks.text: Most of Europe’s wild bee species and about half of its hover fly species have declined over the last century, a study has found, as a UN biodiversity summit begins in Armenia.

Records since 1921 show more bee species are declining than increasing in all parts of Europe except the Alpine region. The richness of bee and hover fly species suffered a persistent drop in the Atlantic and Continental regions, the study found, though trends in other regions were mixed or even positive.

The data, which covers 88% of bee and hover fly species across the continent, suggests pollinator communities have been reshaped by the “gradual loss of sensitive species and the rise of a resilient few”, according to the scientists. They warned of “deeper functional disruptions” if existing trends were not addressed.

Nearly 90% of wild flowering plants, as well as more than three-quarters of major food crop types, depend in part on animal pollination. The UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization has warned the decline of pollinators sets off a chain reaction that threatens wildlife and weakens the ability of ecosystems to withstand climate change and environmental stress.

Carlos Martínez-Núñez, an ecologist at the Spanish National Research Council and lead author of the study, said the findings showed that biodiversity loss could remain hidden behind apparently stable species numbers, “giving us a crucial opportunity to act before further declines occur”.
“The fact that some species are increasing today does not mean they will remain winners as climate change and habitat loss intensify,” he added.

The findings come as diplomats gather in Yerevan for the 17th UN conference on biodiversity. The summit, known as Cop17, will focus on the conservation and sustainable use of the natural world, and the shared benefits of its genetic resources.
after newsletter promotion

The study found 91% of the species logged over the last century had also been recorded at least once in the modern period, between 2001 and 2020. Although this suggests as many as 9% of species could have been wiped out in Europe, many of the species not spotted recently occur only rarely in the historical record, and the researchers said they “do not expect widespread extinctions to have occurred yet”.
However, the species’ occupancy – the probability of being found at a given site – had mostly fallen.

Ainhoa ​​Magrach, an environmental researcher at the Basque Centre for Climate Change (BC3), who was not involved in the study, said it “confirms what has long been suspected: many pollinator species are losing populations, and the decline is not affecting all of them equally”.

“Until now, most of the evidence came from a few north-western European countries, such as the UK, Belgium and the Netherlands,” she said. “This work shows that the pattern extends across the continent, although some regional differences exist.”

Wildlife is dying out at an unprecedented rate as humans destroy habitats, spray pesticides, and warp the weather with planet-heating pollution. Despite far-reaching consequences for humanity, including threats to food systems and further breakdown of the climate, governments have not met a single UN target on nature since the biodiversity convention was created in Rio in 1992.

The Cop17 summit is expected to focus on assessing progress toward this decade’s targets, which include protecting 30% of land and sea, reforming $500bn (£375bn) of environmentally damaging subsidies and restoring 30% of the planet’s degraded ecosystems.

articles.title: DoJ charges 28 green card holders in California over alleged voter fraud
articles.summary:
Crackdown marks latest escalation in the Trump justice department’s push to target alleged noncitizen voting

The US Department of Justice has filed criminal charges against 28 green card…

blocks.text: The US Department of Justice has filed criminal charges against 28 green card holders in California accused of fraudulently registering to vote and casting illegal ballots.

The crackdown marks another escalation in the federal government’s ongoing efforts against alleged noncitizen voting, efforts that Democrats and voting rights groups say are part of a strategy by the Trump administration to sow doubt in the results of the upcoming midterm elections.

The justice department announced Monday that 28 noncitizens from across California were facing charges, including making false statements in a naturalization application and fraudulently signing up to vote, felonies that could carry five years in prison. The defendants are lawful permanent residents, who have legal status in the US but are not citizens authorized to vote.

A justice department spokesperson said 21 of the 28 defendants had cast unlawful ballots. Eleven of the defendants have already been taken into custody and arrests were ongoing, the justice department said. Prosecutors alleged the defendants lied under oath in voter registration applications.
Voting by noncitizens is extremely rare, and election experts have raised concerns that the justice department’s crackdowns could disenfranchise US citizens.

The arrests came days after the justice department sued California, demanding the courts block the state from tabulating certain ballots in the high-stakes November midterms. The justice department had previously sent Los Angeles county election officials a thumb drive that purportedly contained the names of noncitizens who were unlawfully registered to vote. The justice department demanded that California officials, within 48 hours, confirm whether those on the list were citizens and set aside the ballots of those who remained unconfirmed.
The justice department’s lawsuit said it had sent California officials a list of more than 20,000 people who the federal government “believes are likely noncitizens” who were sent ballots by mail.

California’s secretary of state, Shirley Weber, has condemned the justice department’s demands as “outrageous”, saying federal officials had for months made “vague and unsubstantiated allegations” about alleged voter fraud in the state. In a letter last week to the justice department, Weber, a Democrat, noted that the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) first claimed in July that more than 190,000 registered voters in the state “may be” noncitizens, but had since revised that number down to 20,000 while continuing to refuse to share details about its data and methodology.

Weber said that “treating the thousands of voters on DOJ’s list as ineligible until proven otherwise” would violate federal law that prohibits states from systematically removing the names of ineligible voters from voter lists in the lead-up to a federal election.
There are 23.1 million registered voters in California, according to recent state figures.

Trent McCotter, the acting US deputy attorney general, acknowledged the government’s list of alleged noncitizen voters in California might not be accurate when pressed by a reporter to provide more details about the methodology.
“There may be some names on there who, it turns out, ultimately are citizens. We’re not perfect, and that’s why we’ve asked California to cooperate with us,” McCotter said.

On the government’s changing estimates about the volume of allegedly fraudulent registrants in the state, McCotter said: “Think of it like 190,000 is the ceiling, 20,000 is the floor. Twenty-thousand are the ones we’re the most confident about … 190,000 includes ‘medium confidence’, ‘lower confidence’ – kind of the initial cut that have not been manually verified yet.”

McCotter sent a letter to election officials on Friday threatening to prosecute any official that tabulated a ballot from a noncitizen. The threat is legally specious, experts say, and a blatant effort to intimidate officials.

Some federal efforts to root out alleged noncitizen voters have faltered in other states. Last month, Nevada state officials said DHS had wrongly identified 185 people on the state’s voter rolls as noncitizens.
The justice department said Monday that in recent weeks, federal prosecutors have filed charges against a total of 112 people across 20 states for alleged registration offenses and illegal voting.

articles.title: Bulgaria seeks suspects in Germany after Starlink sabotage
articles.summary: A Bulgarian court has issued arrest warrants for two young German nationals suspected of setting fire to Starlink antennae. The case is reminiscent of another in Poland, which Warsaw says was…

image.caption: Separate sabotage attempts took aim at Starlink facilities in Poland and Bulgaria within a matter of weeksImage: Rafapress/Depositphotos/IMAGO

blocks.text: Bulgaria on Monday issued European arrest warrants against two 19-year-old German nationals, saying it suspected their involvement in the sabotage of a series of Starlink antennae near the capital Sofia.

"The evidence gathered makes it possible to conclude that there are reasonable grounds to suspect the involvement of the two defendants," the court in Sofia rules, granting a request from prosecutors.
Ukraine's military uses Starlink's military-grade satellite internet service Starshield for battlefield communications amid Russia's invasion.

Bulgaria does not directly border Ukraine, but it is on the Black Sea, one of the flashpoints of the conflict. A similar case in Poland, which does directly border Ukraine, led to a total of four arrests last week, also in Germany.
What do we know about the incident in Bulgaria?
The two teenage suspects are accused of deliberately setting fire to the antennae on the evening of October 9.
Of 18 in a mountainous region south of Sofia, three were destroyed entirely, two were partially burned and three more were damaged, according to prosecutors.
Prosecutors say the suspects entered from Serbia in a car with German license plates, claiming to be tourists, staying just a few hours around the time of the alleged crime.

Plamen Tonchev, the head of Bulgaria's domestic intelligence agency DANS, said he was working on the assumption that it was deliberate sabotage and said other such acts could not be ruled out in future.
What is the potential tie-in to a Polish sabotage case?
News of the arrests follow just a week after a total of four people were arrested in Germany, accused of sabotaging a Starlink satellite communications station in central Poland in late September.
German police detained three resident men and a woman, two of them Turkish nationals, early last week.
Polish officials said they believed that Russia was behind the sabotage attempt, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk calling it an act of "hybrid warfare."
The domestic intelligence agency also claimed that Russia had cooperated with organized crime elements in Germany on the alleged operation.
Meanwhile, in the Baltic, Lithuania's prime minister on Sunday said that Russia was likely behind an attempted arson attack on a company hosting communication hardware for Starlink satellites.

items: Much ado about Apu: Is The Simpsons character a tired stereotype?
Hank Azaria says stepping away from voicing Apu 'feels like the right thing to do'

blocks.text: Apu's last speaking appearance before his return was in "The Serfsons," which aired in 2017.

The debate over the character's portrayal gained momentum that same year after Indian-American comedian Hari Kondabolu released the documentary, The Problem with Apu, which examines the character's cultural impact and the racial stereotypes critics say he embodies.
"When you see Hank Azaria doing that voice in person ... without the guise of a cartoon, then all of a sudden it's like, that's a white guy making fun of me," Kondabolu says in the documentary.
"It's different all of a sudden, it no longer feels like a character."

On Instagram, Sunil Malhotra shared a photo of himself dressed as Apu beside Janina Gavankar, the voice of Apu's wife, Manjula. Their animated characters appear alongside them beneath a "Homecoming" banner as confetti falls.
"Bringing Apu back feels like a reclamation," Malhotra wrote on Sunday. "It truly IS his homecoming."
Apu's return brings another new voice

Gavankar is also new to The Simpsons, taking over as Manjula from white actor Tress MacNeille. The recasting is part of a broader shift, as the show announced in June 2020 that characters of colour would be voiced by actors of color.
Since then, Alex Désert has taken over as Carl Carlson and Kevin Michael Richardson as Dr. Julius Hibbert. With Malhotra now voicing Apu, the character joins that roster of recast roles.
The Kwik-E-Mart owner's comeback was kept a secret until the episode aired. In Sunday's episode, Apu is revealed as a mysterious figure, then makes his return unmistakable, proclaiming "I am Apu."

The Simpsons showrunner Matt Selman told Variety the character and his family will appear more regularly going forward. "We love this character, and wanted to bring him back in a smart, Simpsons-y way that allowed him to evolve," he said.

In an interview with Variety, Malhotra says he initially had reservations about taking on the role, and wanted to know whether the series could bring Apu back in a way that acknowledged past mistakes.
He said his conversations with Selman and co-executive produxcer Cesar Mazariegos helped reassure him and described recording Apu's emphatic return as a meaningful moment.
CBC News reached out to Selman and Malhotra for comment but has not yet received a response.

Apu's surprise return has received mixed reactions online. Some fans welcomed the character's return. One X user wrote, "Apu is back after almost a decade! Curious to hear Sunil Malhotra bring the character back to life."
Another called the return long overdue, writing that Apu was "one of America's great fictional immigrants," and closed with the character's catchphrase, "#ThankYouComeAgain."
X user @SarahTran68 reacts positively to Apu's return to The Simpsons, writing "Apu is back after almost a decade! Curious to hear Sunil Malhotra bring the character back to life." (SarahTran68/X)
Others questioned the choice.
One X user wrote, "As a brown man, man I miss Hank Azaria as Apu."
Another X user wondered if the show still mattered, writing, "Astounding that anyone still watches. Can't say I've seen an episode in over 20 years. Maybe it's time to just let it go?"

X user @NotFredGwynne calls The Simpsons irrelevant, writing, "Astounding that anyone still watches. Can't say I've seen an episode in over 20 years. Maybe it's time to just let it go?" (NotFredGwynne/X)
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Christine Pagulayan is a Toronto-based producer and writer with CBC News, currently with the Entertainment unit. She has worked in various roles at CBC News Network and The National. She has also worked as a multiplatform reporter in Toronto, Winnipeg, Halifax and Moncton. You can reach her at christine.pagulayan@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Burnham urges officials to come up with more radical options for Thames Water
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Utility seen as ‘litmus test’ of PM’s promise to bring ‘essentials of life’ under public control

Andy Burnham has told officials to rip up their plans for how to fix Thames Water…
articles.byline: Kiran Stacey, Pippa Crerar and Jessica Elgot

blocks.text: Andy Burnham has told officials to rip up their plans for how to fix Thames Water and present him with more radical options for what to do with the stricken company.

In an early test of his promise to bring “the essentials of life” under public control, the prime minister is urging his advisers to go back to the drawing board and create a new list of policies for the utility.
One option being looked at is to convert about £100m of outstanding fines into a government stake in the company, saving its creditors money but giving ministers some say in how it is run.

Burnham previously said he would nationalise Thames, which is running out of cash and recently asked its creditors for an additional £2.4bn, but is struggling to find a way to do so without spending billions of pounds, getting tied up in a lengthy court battle, or both.

Sources familiar with the prime minister’s thinking say he has now told policy officials across Whitehall to contemplate options that were not previously considered feasible, even if that means spending taxpayer money and going to court.

One government source described the fate of the company as a “litmus test” on whether the government could deal with challenges in the medium term, rather than just immediate cost of living support and longer-term structural changes.
“There are more options than people have assumed to date including ones that have never been properly considered,” the source said.
Another said the prime minister had told his officials to “look at all the options and not feel constrained”, in a departure from the advice under Burnham’s predecessor, Keir Starmer.

Burnham has promised to end what he calls “40 years of neoliberalism” and has instructed his ministers to draw up a 10-year plan for government later this year, including detailed proposals for bringing utilities under public control.

Meanwhile, Angela Eagle, the environment secretary, is working on a water bill that will lift a Thatcher-era cap on government ownership of water companies and could rewrite how the bankruptcy regime works for the industry.
Government advisers believe changes to the “special administration regime” (SAR) would make it easier to take companies such as Thames into state control in the future.
But Burnham is also looking for a more immediate solution to Thames’s problems.

When the prime minister came to office, government insiders say he was presented with two main options for Thames: strike a bailout deal with the American hedge funds that own its debt, or pursue an SAR.

Thames’s creditors had proposed a £10bn rescue plan for the company, but Emma Reynolds, the previous environment secretary, made clear her opposition to such a plan before Burnham became prime minister.
Government lawyers also believe it will be difficult to have the company placed into SAR given that it is being kept afloat financially by its creditors and has managed to keep services running.

Among the other options being discussed is the waiving of the approximately £100m in environmental fines the company still owes and taking a stake in it instead. Then, if and when the company is fined again, the government would automatically increase its share rather than collecting the cash.

While some believe this would be a relatively straightforward way to give the government a say in how the company is run, many also believe it would fall short of Burnham’s promise to nationalise the company outright.

The prime minister is under pressure to go further, for example by stripping Thames of its licence, pushing for it to go into SAR immediately and then taking it out of administration without offering anything to the existing creditors.
Such a plan will inevitably be challenged in court, but Burnham is understood to be more willing to take on legal action than Starmer was. One adviser said: “Litigation was always a 100% certainty.”

The prime minister’s advisers also believe they can go further with Thames than with other companies because international investors see the company as a unique case, and not an indication of how the government intends to treat every water company.
Officials say other water companies are likely to be dealt with in different ways, through a mixture of stricter regulation and increased oversight by elected officials such as mayors.

Ewan McGaughey, a professor in law at King’s College, London, said: “The government’s best option is to start a special administration process for Thames Water before it runs up more debts, and sends billions more overseas.
“An orderly transition to public ownership does not require that banks in control are bailed out – on the contrary, the law says polluters should pay.”
Lena Swedlow, deputy director of the Compass campaign group, said: “The obvious solution is to put Thames Water into SAR, and then brought into public ownership so it truly works for everyone.

“While reform of the failing regulatory mechanisms is welcome, any recapitalisation and debt-to-equity schemes that do not seek to permanently wrestle the company from private hands will fail to be in the interests of the workers, stakeholders, and the 16 million people Thames serves. Everything else is noise in the wind.”

articles.title: Police issue curfew in Paris after weekend rioting over cost of living, school conditions
articles.summary: Paris police issued an overnight curfew on Monday in two areas of the French capital in efforts to prevent further violence, after a weekend marred by France's worst rioting in years that targeted…

image.caption: Individuals break a store window during clashes between protesters and police in Paris, Sunday. Police have issued a curfew for parts of Paris Monday. (Emma Da Silva/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

Paris police issued an overnight curfew on Monday in two areas of the French capital in efforts to prevent further violence, after a weekend marred by France's worst rioting in years that targeted city halls, other public buildings and thousands of businesses across the country.
About 3,000 businesses along with other public buildings were damaged or looted across France, police said
The order aims to protect "people and property from the violence and looting," the Paris police statement said.

The curfew prohibits anyone from entering or remaining on the Place de la République, where rioting took place Saturday, and the shopping neighbourhood of Les Halles, which has been subject to looting.
The curfew will be in effect from 11 p.m. local time Monday until 6 a.m. Tuesday. In addition, gatherings and demonstrations are banned from 8 p.m., the Paris police said.
Earlier Monday, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu had called for "very limited" and "localized" curfews.
Protesters burn trash during clashes with police on Sunday. (Emma Da Silva/The Associated Press)

In northern France, local authorities imposed a curfew for children and teenagers under age 18 in several cities, including Lille, starting from Monday and for the next two days from 8 p.m. to 6 a.m. Nice, on the French Riviera, also imposed an overnight curfew for minors from 9 p.m.
Lecornu defended police handling of the unrest, saying that "despite scenes of severe violence and extensive property damage, no one was killed, and that is a miracle."
He said that details of the curfews would be announced later Monday after consultations with mayors.

items: French 'lycée' protests spread to Quebec as Montreal students take to streets in solidarity
Student-led protesters clash with riot police in France

blocks.text: Mass protests in France are often tainted by violence on the fringes of otherwise peaceful marches, leading to clashes with police.

Saturday's unrest recalled the riots that followed the fatal police shooting of a teenager in 2023, when authorities imposed local curfews, and violence during the yellow vest movement that began in 2018 over fuel prices and broader economic grievances.
A worker repairs a window of a looted shop following the riots. (Christophe Ena/The Associated Press)
Macron rejects minister's resignation

The prime minister's instructions come after France's interior minister Laurent Nuñez offered his resignation Sunday. But President Emmanuel Macron refused it "given the need for continued command of law enforcement in the current context," Macron's office said in a statement Monday.
He instructed Nuñez "to take all necessary steps to ensure full transparency about the failures in planning and intelligence-gathering that led to the violence," the statement said.
Macron also asked for the introduction of "new policing tactics on the ground as quickly as possible" to put an end to the violence.

items: France shaken by fiery street protests uniting students, workers and 'yellow vests'

blocks.text: On Sunday evening, groups set fire to trash bins, bicycles and other objects in the streets and looted businesses in Paris, Lyon, Marseille and other cities. That followed the violence during nationwide protests Saturday against rising living costs and poor conditions in schools. At least 2,400 people were arrested across the country.
Authorities estimated Monday that at least 3,000 businesses were damaged or looted in several cities.
In Marseille, the prefect banned any protest or other gatherings from noon to 8 p.m. Monday.

"I submitted my resignation because I am responsible for everything that is happening," Nuñez said on France Inter radio. "Now the real issue is ensuring that this doesn't happen again. … We obviously need to be better at anticipating the kind of mobilization that is unfolding."
Nuñez blamed the violence on "hordes of troublemakers and looters" and "far-left activists," and said that police strategy needs to be adapted "in the face of extremely mobile groups."
Authorities said that groups of hundreds of people sought confrontations with police and targeted public buildings, including city halls and other public offices.
A man throws a plastic traffic cone through a burning barricade amid clashes Saturday in Paris. (Abdul Saboor/Reuters)
Authorities 'lost control,' says minister
Nuñez acknowledged that authorities had "lost control" in some major cities on Saturday.
"You can't look shopkeepers in the eye when hundreds of businesses have been looted and say we haven't lost control in some of these major cities," Nuñez said.
Flames engulfed the 19th-century City Hall in Limoges, in central France, causing its roof to collapse and nearly destroying the building.
On Monday, clean-up crews and firefighters cleared shattered glass and other debris from the streets of Paris.
Ouri Zagoury, owner of a video game shop near Paris' Place de la République, said that he closed the store Saturday afternoon, but then saw looters forcing their way in on surveillance cameras.
"There were so many people coming in and out. And even though I called the police, they said not to intervene, that they would come, but they never did, which is another problem," Zagoury said.
Jordan Bardella, president of the far-right National Rally party, pointed to the government's failure to prevent violence.
"The government has failed, the head of state has failed in his essential duty of protecting the French people," he told reporters at the party's headquarters.

"I call on the people of France now, beyond their right to protest, to use their voting power," Bardella said. He is campaigning alongside far-right leader Marine Le Pen, whose polling numbers have suggested for months that she's the front-runner in next spring's presidential election.

articles.title: Ukrainians dying because US restricting intelligence sharing, Zelensky adviser tells BBC
articles.summary: Serhii Beskrestnov says there has not been enough time to warn people about incoming missile attacks.

blocks.text: Ukrainians have died because Kyiv is still not receiving reliable US warnings of incoming Russian attacks, according to a key adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky.

Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov told the BBC that lives had been lost because there had not been time to warn citizens about ballistic missile strikes, saying: "It's dangerous... I think it's really very bad... People [have] already died."
The adviser also said restrictions to Ukraine's use of the Starlink internet network were ongoing.
The White House said there had been no changes to intelligence sharing with Ukraine.
Ukraine first reported an interruption to US intelligence sharing last week, as a row with the Trump administrations over its controversial deal to import Russian oil sent relations to new lows.
Despite the denials from Washington, many in Kyiv suspect the Starlink issues are not a coincidence.
On Monday morning, Zelensky wrote on social media: "Overnight two ballistic missile attacks were reported on the capital, one without warning, the second with only minimal time to take shelter."
Hours earlier, an interview the president did with NBC was published, in which he said intelligence sharing had been restored after a three-day pause.
"We are very thankful for this," he said. "Only [the] United States has this unique intelligence to tell our side when Russia uses ballistic missiles."
But Beskrestnov told the BBC that American intelligence continued to be incomplete and inconsistent, and that the US had failed to provide a clear explanation for the issue.
"This looks very strange," he said. "Sometimes we receive this information before the attack, another time we [do] not."
He continued: "And for example, last night we received it, but... one minute before the attack."
However, he said other collaboration with US continues, adding: "Intelligence data keeps flowing, and the issue is solely with the air raid alert component."

Beskrestnov also said the US had given no clarity about who was responsible for the ongoing restrictions to the Starlink internet network and its military service Starshield, which Kyiv uses to provide connectivity for drones, helicopters and military communications.
Last week, Starshield restricted the speed at which mobile units could move while staying connected to the network to 100mph (160km/h).
This has limited Ukraine's ability to shoot down incoming drones or to launch mid-range drone attacks into Russian-occupied areas.

Starlink owner Elon Musk said last week that the US government ultimately controls access to Starshield, which was designed for the Pentagon, suggesting it may therefore be behind the restrictions. Trump has denied involvement.
Beskrestnov said he thought both issues occurring at the same time was "probably" a deliberate move to put pressure on Ukraine.
He told BBC News: "It's probably the United States trying to say [to] us, 'let's have the conversation, negotiation with Russia, you should find the compromise'."
Beskrestnov also said Ukraine had its own radar data to provide some limited warning of incoming attacks, but was urgently looking into using alternative communication systems.
He added: "Now we understand that something begins to happen with Starlink, and we're not sure what will be the next step.

"We understand that we should be prepared for some problems in future. And now we're thinking about an alternative for Starlink, not only for air defence, for communication between our forces, between our staff, for civilians also, because we don't know what we should expect in future regarding Starlink."
Earlier on Monday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there had not been a "pause" to intelligence sharing.
"I don't know where [Zelensky is] getting these things or why he's saying these things to the press," he told reporters on Monday.
Rubio said he could not comment on the incident, adding: "I know a few nights ago there was a software problem involving their early warning system."
The BBC has contacted Starlink for a response.
A White House official said there were no changes to intelligence sharing operations between the US and Ukraine.
The official spoke on background to discuss intelligence matters. Trump is focused on ending the war, the official said, and added that the US has provided more aid to Ukraine than any other country.

articles.title: France imposes partial curfews in several cities, including parts of Paris
articles.summary: Interior minister concedes police ‘lost control’ of weekend protests and says he is ‘fully resolved to restore public order’

blocks.text: Partial curfews have been issued for a number of French cities, including parts of Paris, after the government admitted police had “lost control” during violent weekend protests around the country.

Sébastien Lecornu, the French prime minister, said after an emergency cabinet meeting on Monday he was “fully resolved to restore public order” and had called for “local and partial” curfews if needed. There was “no question” of imposing a full curfew on entire cities, he said.
His office later announced partial curfews from 8pm to 6am on Monday and Tuesday nights in four northern cities, including Lille.

Police also imposed a curfew from 11pm Monday until 6am on Tuesday on two locations in Paris: Place de la République, where rioting took place Saturday; and the shopping neighbourhood of Les Halles, which has been subject to looting.
A statement from police said the orders banned gatherings and demonstrations and prohibited anyone from entering or remaining in the two designated areas.

France’s second city, Marseille, earlier announced independently that it had banned all gatherings and demonstrations on Monday. French unions, meanwhile, called for a new ⁠round of strikes and rallies on 5 November.
Lecornu told reporters that if declaring a state of emergency was deemed necessary “we could do so”, but ⁠added that at this stage partial curfews seemed “more appropriate”.

Lecornu’s comments came after France’s interior minister conceded that police had “lost control” in some cities during Saturday’s protests and the president, Emmanuel Macron, demanded a full security review and “new operational methods” to end the rioting.

Laurent Nuñez said on Monday there had been a “lack of anticipation” in preparations for the protests and acknowledged that police numbers had sometimes been inadequate to deal with rioters and looters on the fringes of the demonstrations.

Nuñez said intelligence had suggested there would be 200,000 demonstrators around the country. In the event, there were more than 500,000 and peaceful protests were hijacked, morphing into one of France’s most violent days of unrest in recent years.

He said he had tendered his resignation to Macron because he felt “responsible for everything that happened”. Macron refused it, demanding instead that Nuñez “take all necessary steps to ensure transparency over planning and intelligence failures”.

blocks.caption: Laurent Nuñez, the interior minister, offered his resignation to Emmanuel Macron, which was declined. Photograph: Julien de Rosa/Pool AFP/AP

blocks.text: The protests follow weeks of demonstrations by high school students that have been marred by sometimes violent clashes with police, rocking the country six months before a crunch presidential ⁠election and amid mounting economic pressures.

Public buildings including a town hall were attacked and set ablaze and an estimated 2,000 shops were ransacked and looted, authorities have said. Nearly 2,400 people – 70% of them adults – were arrested and almost 1,000 police and gendarmes injured.

France’s digital minister, Anne Le Henanff, urged online resale platforms to remove listings for “stolen items” and summoned representatives of companies including Vinted and eBay. According to the commerce ministry, representatives of Amazon, Leboncoin, Meta and TikTok were also invited.

Nuñez said 60,000 police and other security forces had been deployed around the country, but acknowledged it had not been enough to control determined, organised groups of violent rioters in major cities including Paris, Marseille and Lyon.

“You couldn’t look shopkeepers in the eye after hundreds of shops had been looted and say we hadn’t lost control,” the minister told French radio, but added that the responsibility of “rioters, looters and ultra-left militants” should not be glossed over.

The justice minister, Gérald Darmanin, also said intelligence failings had left the state vulnerable. “There’s no good policing without good intelligence, he said, adding that many of those arrested had police records and “about 80%” were being prosecuted.

blocks.caption: An estimated 2,000 shops were ransacked and looted across France during the rioting. Photograph: Carl Court/Getty Images

blocks.text: Macron’s office said in a statement on Monday that besides reviewing the security shortcomings, Nuñez had been tasked with “promptly implementing new operational methods for security forces to use on the ground in combating rioters”.

Rioting and looting continued on Sunday. The mayor of Paris, Emmanuel Grégoire, said on Monday that about 30 shops had been targeted in the capital the previous day, with a further 350 people arrested overnight.

“Maintaining public order is the responsibility of the state. It is the state that was at fault this weekend,” Grégoire said. “We have a social movement that is spreading, and no political prospect for a constructive way out. So the protests will continue.”

Marseille’s mayor, Benoît Payan, said not just democracy but “the very foundations of the Republic” had been undermined. Describing the situation as “almost insurrectional”, he said the government’s stance amounted to “petty political manoeuvring”.

blocks.caption: The Louvre was unable to open as scheduled on Monday because of protesters blocking its entrance. Photograph: Abdul Saboor/Reuters

blocks.text: On Monday, protesters blocked entrances to the Louvre Museum in support of the nationwide high school student protest movement and to denounce “police repression”. The museum could not open as scheduled because of the protest.
A leaflet displayed outside the museum read: “We are proud to announce that we are blocking the world’s largest museum.”

In a televised address on Sunday, Macron criticised the “unbridled” violence and said local authorities would be able to ban some demonstrations in the coming days, but stopped short of drastic measures such as declaring a state of emergency or curfew.

Saturday’s protests, by students, teachers, parents, unions and workers, focused on the high cost of living, an issue that also prompted demonstrations in several other European countries including Italy, Belgium and Albania over the weekend.

articles.title: Israeli police detain 10 people in rare raid against West Bank settlers
articles.summary:
Move comes after US photojournalist and group of European diplomats and Palestinians were assaulted in separate attacks

Israeli police have detained 10 people in a rare raid against…

blocks.text: Israeli police have detained 10 people in a rare raid against settlers, after a weekend of extreme violence in the occupied West Bank including an attack on US photojournalist Heidi Levine, which she described as an “attempted lynching”.

She was knocked down, kicked and beaten by a group of masked Israeli men as she covered the olive harvest in a Palestinian village on Friday. The militants broke four vertebrae and a rip, ripped open her finger so it required surgery and left her with lacerations across her body.
“I was practically, basically lynched by a gang of Jewish settlers in the area of Ramallah,” Levine said, in an interview with the BBC from her hospital bed on Monday.

The day after that assault, Israeli militants armed with sticks and iron bars attacked a group of European diplomats and Palestinians harvesting olives outside the town of Taybeh, assaulting a visiting French mayor, smashing the window of an official car, and causing severe injuries to a young Palestinian man.
The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, questioned the accounts of Israeli militant violence, ignoring extensive video and witness evidence.
He referenced an “alleged attack” on Levine, whose severe injuries were visible in interviews from her hospital bed, and “unproven allegations” the diplomats had been targeted by militants.

The attacks and his response drew a furious international reaction, including from the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee – generally considered a staunch ally of the current Israeli government – European nations and the editor of the Washington Post, Matt Murray.
On Monday morning Israeli police released footage of a rare raid on settlers, and said they had detained 10 people connected with the attacks on foreigners and construction of an illegal outpost.
Hours later a court extended the detention of six men connected with the attacks on foreigners, to between three and four days.
There has been little response to extreme violence against Palestinians across the West Bank, and Levine said the global focus on her attack highlighted extreme double standards.
“People are dealing with this, undergoing attacks, losing property, losing family members, being injured all across the West Bank and nothing is being done,” she said.
Israelis target Palestinians with near total impunity in the occupied West Bank, where arrests are unusual, indictments rare and convictions even more unusual.

Israeli human rights group Yesh Din has documented 561 incidents of settler and soldier violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank over three weeks since 27 September. That is an average of more than 26 each day.

“It is telling that it took attacks on foreign nationals to prompt a significant response from Israeli authorities,” said the group’s executive director, Ziv Stahl. “Palestinians have endured years of systematic settler violence, with 94% of investigations into cases of settler violence against Palestinians closed without indictments.

Levine said her body armour and helmet had prevented even more serious injuries, and she considered herself “lucky” given the ferocity of the attack. Netanyahu’s attempt to cast doubt on the attack felt like a “a big slap on my face”, she added.

Netanyahu’s statements, apparently undermined by security forces arrests days later, were widely seen as an attempt to court far-right voters inside Israel, as the country heads into the final days of an election campaign.

His coalition partners include extremist settlers, who support the campaign of violence that has driven thousands of Palestinians from their homes and land in the occupied West Bank over the last three years.

Haaretz reported on Monday that political pressure was preventing the army from confronting “Jewish terrorism” in the West Bank, even when the targets were foreigners including diplomats and journalists.
Commanders are reluctant to challenge settler leaders, or take action against Israeli civilians and soldiers who attack Palestinians, Israeli defence officials told the paper.
Formal investigations and disciplinary procedures are limited and undermined by unofficial but clear messages of support from top commanders, the report said.

It cited the response to an attack on a CNN crew in March. Central Command chief Maj Gen Avi Bluth suspended the battalion responsible from operational duty and announced disciplinary action against soldiers involved.
Later that night, the brigade commander came to a base where the soldiers were staying to express his support and join them in prayer, Haaretz said.
