articles.title: Former Winnipeg mayor Sam Katz violated public trust, ex-CAO lacked moral compass, police HQ inquiry says
articles.summary: Former Winnipeg mayor Sam Katz “violated the public trust” and former city chief administrative officer Phil Sheegl displayed “a complete lack of a moral compass” by engaging in "blatant" conflicts…

blocks.text: Head of Winnipeg police HQ inquiry releases final report

Former Winnipeg mayor Sam Katz "violated the public trust" and former chief administrative officer Phil Sheegl displayed "a complete lack of a moral compass" by engaging in "blatant" conflicts of interest involving the owner of the construction company that built the city's police headquarters, the provincial public inquiry into the scandal-plagued project concluded.

That owner, Armik Babakhanians of Caspian Construction, engaged in "unethical conduct" through his efforts to secure the police headquarters work — and then proceeded to inflate construction costs by $42 million and increase his company's profits, the inquiry found.

In a 193-page report published Monday, inquiry commissioner Garth Smorang castigates Katz, Sheegl, Babakhanians, other Caspian officials and several Caspian subcontractors for their roles in the procurement, management, oversight and funding of the police headquarters project.

In his report, entitled A Sad Tale of Mismanagement, Misconduct and Misrepresentations, Smorang singles out the former mayor and CAO in particular for engaging in financial transactions with Babakhanians while the city was in the process of choosing a construction company to work on the police headquarters project.

"Both Sheegl and Katz testified that their relationships with Armik had no impact on their decisions. However, it bears repeating that the reason that conflicts of interest are so insidious is that the public can never be confident that the decisions taken were free from bias," Smorang wrote.
"The conflicts of interest under which Katz and Sheegl operated were so blatant that there will always be questions. Unfortunately, those questions will never be able to be answered."
Cash exchange 'papered over' as land deal

The police headquarters project involved the 2009 city purchase of a former Canada Post office and warehouse complex in downtown Winnipeg and its subsequent conversion into the new home of the Winnipeg Police Service, which opened in 2016.
The $209-million project was completed two years late and $74 million over budget, according to inquiry accounting. Earlier media arithmetic had pegged those figures as $5 million higher each.

The project was also plagued by procurement and management issues that spawned two city audits, a five-year RCMP investigation into fraud, forgery and secret commissions and a pair of lawsuits that recouped more than $29 million for the city.

One of those lawsuits resulted in two Manitoba courts concluding Sheegl accepted a $327,200 bribe from Babakhanians to ensure Caspian was awarded the police headquarters work — and that Sheegl later shared half the money with Katz.

items: Former Winnipeg CAO Phil Sheegl loses appeal, must pay $1.1M for accepting bribe from police HQ contractor

blocks.text: While Smorang was not instructed to reconsider the court conclusions, the commissioner rejected testimony from Sheegl, Katz and Babakhanians that they exchanged money in 2011 and 2012 as part of an Arizona land transaction.
"I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that they entered into a financial transaction whereby Armik paid $327,200 to Sheegl and Katz, which was then split equally between them," Smorang wrote.

"Armik identified the first $200,000 payment as 'consulting services' in his accounting of the money. Sheegl then passed on $100,000 to Katz, which was stated to be a 'loan.' This financial transaction was at some later time papered over and explained by all three as a land transaction."
Smorang noted Katz voted in favour of two motions "that directly benefited Armik and Caspian."

The first was a July 2011 city council motion to increase the budget for the police headquarters project by $50 million. The second was a January 2013 motion to increase the budget by a further $16 million.
The inquiry into the construction of Winnipeg's police headquarters project heard from 30 witnesses between February and May of 2026. (CBC)

Smorang said Sheegl "participated in many decisions" that benefited Babakhanians, including the decision to award a $137-million police headquarters construction contract to Caspian the day after Sheegl became CAO in 2011.

Smorang also noted Sheegl made the decision not to invite other companies to bid on the work after a joint venture between Caspian and Akman Construction — who were jointly awarded a $50,000 initial construction management contract — fell apart.

Sheegl also made the decision to remove AECOM, the initial construction firm responsible for the project design, in favour of Peter Chang of consulting firm Adjeleian Allen Rubeli, who had ties to Babakhanians, Smorang wrote.
Sheegl also requested Babakhanians arrange for a subcontractor to build an $8,500 deck at the CAO's home in 2013, at no cost to Sheegl, Smorang said.
Bonding change allowed Caspian in
Smorang also chronicled how Sheegl was involved in a pivotal city decision that allowed Caspian to bid on the police headquarters work in the first place.

In October 2010, Sheegl and Katz met with Babakhanians and his son Shaun Babakhanians at high-end steakhouse 529 Wellington to "discuss possible business arrangements," said an email from Armik to Shaun Babakhanians, according to inquiry testimony and the report.
The same fall, the city was searching for a construction manager for the project and had originally set a December 2010 deadline for companies to bid on the work, the report says.

The request for proposals included a standard provision that bidders would secure a 50 per cent performance bond, which is money construction companies put up to ensure they're able to complete construction work after it gets underway.

Two days before the bid was slated to close, Armik Babakhanians asked the city to reduce the bonding requirement. At the inquiry, the Caspian owner testified he could not meet the requirement and had to borrow $1 million to qualify for the bond.
After a city engineer balked at the change, Sheegl wrote to deputy Winnipeg CAO Alex Robinson to intervene before then-mayor Katz got involved.

"I just know his next call is to Sam and the comment to me from Sam will be 'They are strong enough for Canada Post and the Department of National Defence but we can't figure it out.' PLEASE make this thing work," Sheegl wrote.

"If there is any single event that might be seen as the event that changed the course of history in relation to this project, it would be this email. Without this email, the bonding requirements would not have been changed, and Caspian would not have been able to bid on the project," Smorang wrote.
"Instead, the bond was changed and the rest of the sad story unfolded."

items: City lowered bond amount for Winnipeg police HQ project despite warning of risk, inquiry hears

blocks.text: Other pivotal decisions that doomed the project included the failure of Sheegl and other members of the police HQ project steering team to assign a team of people to support initial police HQ project manager Abdul Aziz or initially free him up from his existing duties managing police facilities.
"The project began under the direction of an individual who was dedicated to the success of the project, but who was put into an impossible situation by the lack of proper resources," Smorang wrote.

Abdul Aziz, the director of services for the Winnipeg Police Service, testified at the inquiry into the Winnipeg police headquarters project on Feb. 23. He is one of four public servants who received praise from inquiry commissioner for trying to prevent the city from rash actions. (Bartley Kives/CBC)

A second flaw from the start was the decision to attempt to procure, design and build the headquarters in the space of only three years, which witnesses at the inquiry said was as an extremely abbreviated timeline for a construction project of this size and complexity.

Other major blunders included proceeding to negotiate a "guaranteed maximum price" contract with Caspian based on building designs that were only 30 per cent complete, the removal of both Aziz and AECOM from the project and a final decision to provide Caspian with more funds in 2013, Smorang wrote.
$43.3 million in inflated costs

Smorang also concluded the increased cost of the project was not solely due to mismanagement. Armik Babakhanians, he said, "set out right from the start of the project to inflate Caspian's costs," to the city's detriment.

Smorang said Armik, his son Shaun and Caspian employee Pam Anderson "engaged in a planned and systematic process of creating false and misleading documents, for the purpose of improperly inflating Caspian's purported costs and increasing Caspian's profits."
The three Caspian officials "acted in bad faith and in complete disregard of their obligation to treat the City of Winnipeg with candor and honesty," Smorang said.

items: Falsifying police HQ project invoices was wrong, former Caspian director tells inquiry

blocks.text: They created false invoices and false quotations with inflated amounts, claimed invoices that they did not pay to their subtrades, included costs for other projects as part of the police-headquarters claim, and claimed invoices from subtrades that didn't do the invoiced work, the report said.
"It was puzzling throughout this inquiry to hear from several small business owners who got caught up in Armik's schemes without receiving a tangible benefit," the commissioner said.
Smorang concluded these actions resulted in $42 million in inflated payments to Caspian.

He concluded an additional $1.3-million overpayment was made when police HQ funds were diverted through a shell company to Caspian employee Anderson, Chang of Adjeleian Allen Rubeli and Patrick Dubuc of GRC Architects.
Commissioner makes 25 recommendations
Neither Chang nor Dubuc testified at the inquiry. Smorang said he could not compel them to testify because they do not reside in Manitoba.
Among 25 recommendations, Smorang advised the province to change interprovincial subpoena legislation so public inquiries can compel people living outside Manitoba to testify, as courts can do now.

Smorang also recommended the City of Winnipeg expand the powers of its integrity commissioner to scrutinize senior city bureaucrats and not just elected officials. He also advised the province to change provincial legislation to make Winnipeg's integrity commissioner a statutory officer able to investigate tips from the public.
Smorang recommended the city amend its conflict of interest policies to ensure any official who awards a sole-sourced contract disclose any relationship with the recipient of that contract.
He also suggested city council's executive policy committee should provide oversight of major projects, which are defined as any project with a value between $100 million and $499 million.
Smorang also recommended Manitoba Prosecution Service be "more open and forthcoming" in its media releases about why the Crown decides not to pursue charges in high-profile investigations.
The RCMP spent five years investigating the police headquarters project and did not lay any charges.

items: RCMP were prepared to make arrests in Winnipeg police HQ construction project: briefing note

blocks.text: "Since being appointed in February 2025, no other question has been asked of me more often by friends, neighbours, former colleagues, lawyers and judges than — why weren't criminal charges laid in this case?" Smorang said.
"This is particularly so since the media has ably reported the evidence heard at the public hearings."
Lawyer Danny Gunn and his client, former Winnipeg mayor Sam Katz, prepare for a public hearing at the Winnipeg police headquarters inquiry on Feb. 12. (Rudi Pawlychyn/CBC)
Smorang said it was not up to him to question decisions made by the Crown. He had no mandate to revisit the RCMP investigation or other examinations of the police headquarters project.

That included a 2014 real estate audit by consulting firm EY, which noted the city did not consider any potential location for its new police headquarters other than the Canada Post complex, and a separate 2014 construction audit that concluded the project was mismanaged.
Smorang did single out four city employees for their efforts to protect the city "from rash acts of others" that went ignored while the police headquarters saga unfolded.

Winnipeg Police Service facilities manager Aziz, city purchasing manager Barb D'Avignon, city finance manager Jason Ruby and retired police inspector Randy Benoit "deserve special recognition," Smorang wrote.

He also praised members of city council and public servants for pursuing legal action against Sheegl in the court proceedings that determined he accepted a $327,200 bribe from Babakhanians. This allowed the city to recover nearly $1.2 million from the former CAO.
A second city lawsuit against Babakhanians and other defendants was settled for $28 million.

items: Caspian owner needed $33M high-interest mortgage to pay police HQ settlement

blocks.text: "There was great determination showed by city officials, both elected and appointed, who pursued multiple legal avenues to recover the money that was owed. They are rightly deserving of both congratulations and thanks," Smorang said.
Thirty witnesses testified during 27.5 days of police HQ inquiry public hearings held from February to May. The inquiry had a $2.3-million budget.

articles.title: ITV’s exposé of racism and misogyny in Reform? Just a few (more) bad apples | John Crace
articles.summary:
While the party’s MPs went into hiding, it was left to its failed byelection candidate Matt Goodwin to defend it

It was the dog that didn’t bark in the night. After Sunday night’s ITV

blocks.text: It was the dog that didn’t bark in the night. After Sunday night’s ITV exposé of widespread racism and misogyny within Reform, you might have expected one of its MPs to have taken to the airwaves on Monday morning to defend the party’s honour. To try to persuade viewers that the real problem lay with the journalists who couldn’t stop themselves from investigating Reform rather than the fact that the party’s bigotry was endemic.

Instead, we got nothing. Every Reform MP was otherwise engaged. Were too busy having breakfast. Nothing from Nigel Farage. Nothing even from Robert Jenrick. Maybe he realised he had crashed and burned a few days earlier by suggesting it was just one of those things. One of life’s little mysteries. The BBC was riddled with paedophiles and Reform was awash with racists, said Honest Bob. No big deal. Every organisation had its crosses to bear.

The only MP to take to X in the morning was Richard Tice, who was feeling decidedly grumpy having only just got married to Isabel Oakeshott. Perhaps he had a hangover. Though his main gripe was that British Airways was yet another failing British institution because it had mislaid at least one of his bags.

Dicky’s social media post had more than a touch of the “don’t you know who I am” to it. You can only imagine the baggage handler may have known exactly who Dicky was and had taken great pleasure in diverting one of the fake Louis Vuitton suitcases from Dubai to Manila. Via Buenos Aires.

The one person out and about for Reform was the one person you would have thought the party would want to keep hidden. Step forward Matt Goodwin, the party’s failed candidate for the Gorton and Denton byelection whose own views could easily pass off as borderline racist in polite circles. Matt is going through his own personal anti-growth agenda. Working hard to deconstruct himself from low-level academic to incredibly dim primate with low social skills. Almost every day, voters in Gorton and Denton thank their lucky stars for having dodged a bullet.

Matt’s defence of Reform was … unorthodox. To put it kindly. So much so that you began to wonder whether he was even conscious. Luckily for him, he was only allowed out on Times Radio. Though that was more than enough. To try to understand Matt is to make a category error. The whole point is to not understand him. That’s the way you stay sane. Because what he wanted listeners to believe was that Nige was a buffer zone against racism. That hordes of would-be racists begged to be allowed to join Reform, only to find out that Nige was a man of peace and love. The one politician who wanted nothing but good things for all immigrants.

It got better. Because Batshit Matt also wanted us to believe that the ITV documentary had just uncovered a few bad apples in the party. So in a way had done Reform a favour. What were the chances? The ITV journalists had managed to uncover the only seven racists in the Reform ranks. Everyone else was Team Nigel. Never had a bad word for anyone. Except, there was another way of looking at this. That ITV had filmed about 10 Reform councillors and found that seven of them had views that included beheading King Charles for being a Muslim. Some statisticians might put that down as a 70% hit rate. Not so much a few wrong uns but a whole army of them. Poor Nige. Always the victim.
after newsletter promotion

Over in the Commons, Wes Streeting was preparing for other threats during departmental defence questions. Though John Healey was not one of them. You’d have thought that Wes might have wanted to schmooze the chancellor before next week’s budget. To try to get the best funding settlement he could. Not a bit of it. Wes began by slagging off his predecessor as defence secretary for wasting money on unnecessary training exercises and then announced he was confident that Healey would reach the necessary 3% and 3.5% targets at next year’s spending review. So, no, Wes wouldn’t be resigning any time soon. Let’s hope his confidence is well placed.

Instead, Wes seemed more interested in persuading himself that there was absolutely nothing unusual in Donald Trump switching the Starlink satellite system on and off at random moments, thereby allowing Russian drones to do untold damage on Ukraine. This was just standard procedure. The only way you could tell the system was working properly was if you turned it off from time to time. Obvious when you think about. Wes was also totally chilled about Trump trying to lower US pump prices by allowing Russian imports of diesel. Fuel that the Russians had also imported from Iran and with whom, coincidentally, the US was at war.

All of this apparently made perfect sense not just to Streeting, but also to Labour and opposition backbenchers. Wes could reassure us because he had had a personal meeting with Pete Hegseth the previous week, during with the secretary for war had reiterated Trump’s claims that Nato forces had been a waste of space in Afghanistan and that the US troops had fought alone. A nice ice breaker. After that Pete went out of his way to say Washington was totally behind Ukraine, just so long as Russia won the war.

Curiously, the shadow defence secretary, James Cartlidge, didn’t use his questions to talk up the four drones of the “Britannia shield” that the Tories were sure would protect the UK from nuclear war. So it remains a mystery. Almost as if it was a bullshit party conference announcement that was designed to be forgotten within days. Highlight of the day went to Sharron Davies, the former swimmer turned Tory peer, who demanded to know why Andy Burnham hadn’t invaded France to stop the rioting. Can you explain it to her?

articles.title: Massachusetts lieutenant governor candidate ends campaign after arrest
articles.summary:
Police said Shawn Oliver was arrested on suspicion of operating under influence of alcohol after a car crash

The Republican candidate for lieutenant governor in

blocks.text: The Republican candidate for lieutenant governor in Massachusetts announced the suspension of his campaign on Sunday hours after he was arrested in a suspected drunk-driving crash.
Shawn Oliver, a city councilor in New Bedford and a corrections officer, said in a post on X he was ending his campaign because “the election is too important to be overshadowed by personal matters”.

The move came after Mike Minogue, his running mate and a Republican gubernatorial candidate, said he asked Oliver to immediately suspend his campaign and that “when elected, I will formally ask for his resignation”.
“I am extremely disappointed,” Minogue said on X. “There is no excuse for driving under the influence.”
Police said Oliver, 42, was arrested after he was involved in a car crash late on Saturday involving a vehicle that struck multiple parked vehicles before turning over.

He was taken to the hospital for injuries and arrested on suspicion of operating under the influence of alcohol, negligent operation of a motor vehicle, a marked lanes violation and speeding, said Holly Huntoon, a police spokesperson, in an email.
The arrest was first reported by the New Bedford Light.

Oliver appeared in court on Monday, and a judge suspended his driver’s license, the New England news outlet WJAR reported. WJAR reported that the judge also released Oliver from custody on his own recognizance – meaning he wasn’t required to post a bail bond – pending the outcome of the case.
Jon Mitchell, New Bedford’s Democratic mayor, said the allegations against Oliver were “deeply concerning” and that the public deserved to hear from him about what happened.

A phone message seeking comment was left for Oliver, who was born and raised in New Bedford, a city of 100,000 people about 60 miles (97km) south of Boston. He was elected to the city council in 2023.
Minogue, a businessman and military veteran, faces incumbent Democratic governor Maura Healey on the 3 November ballot. The Democratic candidate for lieutenant governor is incumbent Kim Driscoll.
“Shawn is lucky to be alive and lucky that no one innocent was hurt,” said Minogue’s X post after Oliver’s arrest.
The lieutenant governor’s position in Massachusetts is seen as largely ceremonial. But the officeholder is first in line to become governor if the governor resigns or dies.

Oliver has been placed on restricted work duty at his job at the Massachusetts Treatment Center “while all facts and circumstances are reviewed”, said an email from Lindsay Corcoran, a state department of correction spokesperson. The medium-security facility houses sex offenders and people civilly committed as sexually dangerous persons.

articles.title: Quebec's reserves of maple syrup almost depleted, says new report
articles.summary: The head of Quebec's maple syrup producers' association says the province's strategic syrup reserve has run dry amid high demand for the product.

image.caption: Cans of maple syrup wait to be processed at Érablière Côté et Fils in Roxton Pond, Que., on Monday, March 9. (Christinne Muschi/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Montreal·New
The head of Quebec's maple syrup producers' association says the province's strategic syrup reserve has run dry amid high demand for the product.
Province's producers ask government for financial support, help finding new markets abroad
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Oct 19, 2026 1:41 PM EDT | Last Updated: 16 minutes ago
Québec Maple Syrup Producers president Luc Goulet says government support will be needed to ensure the industry doesn't miss out on opportunities to grow the sector.
Maple syrup yields depend on weather conditions. As a result, the producers' association has established a strategic reserve to ensure prices and supply remain relatively stable.
Last year, U.S. commercial customers stocked up, fearing that U.S. President Donald Trump would carry out his threat to impose tariffs.

items: Fake maple syrup class action now targeting major grocery store chains

blocks.text: Goulet says the buffer has been exhausted as sales continue to rise.
"Our strategic reserve has been reduced to zero," Goulet said in an interview at the release of a report on the industry's economic benefits.
That means the industry could lose customers if weather conditions are less favourable for maple sap flow, he said.
Goulet cites the stock shortages in 2007 and 2008 as an example.

"We lost some markets because the product wasn’t available," Goulet said. "Then, consumers very quickly turn to another sweet product. And once that happens, those consumption habits are established."

items: Canada is unlocking its maple syrup vault. Here's what it looks like

blocks.text: Quebec maple syrup is gaining market share abroad, according to the president of the Maple Industry Council, which represents authorized buyers.

Louis Turenne notes that exports increased by 9.34 per cent in 2024 compared to the previous year. The pace accelerated in 2025 with a 15.8 per cent increase as the threat of new tariffs loomed over the industry.
In 2026, exports rose at a slower rate — 2.48 per cent from January through August compared to the same period the previous year.
"It's always hard to beat an exceptional year," Turenne said.
Currently, nearly 65 per cent of maple syrup exports go to the United States. (Christinne Muschi/The Canadian Press)
Goulet acknowledges that satisfying the demand of eager consumers is a nice problem to have.
However, he believes the industry can still grow. "There is still a great deal of untapped potential in Quebec’s maple groves," he said.
Investments from Quebec City "are too low for our liking," says Goulet, who hopes to have the ear of the newly elected Parti Québécois government.
"When we’re told that we have an industry that's thriving, that we’re growing, and that we don’t need support — well, I no longer accept that line of reasoning at the government level," he said.
For his part, Turenne believes that Quebec could encourage increased production by providing financial support to producers, and helping processors in their search for new markets abroad.
Currently, nearly 65 per cent of maple syrup exports go to the United States.
"We’ve made significant progress in diversifying our markets in recent years. Twenty years ago, that figure was 80 per cent," Turenne said.
“But we need to accelerate the opening and development of European, Australian, and Asian markets to become less dependent on the U.S. market,” he said.
Industry concentrated in Quebec
While the maple leaf graces the Canadian flag, the syrup industry is heavily concentrated in Quebec.
More than 70 per cent of North American production is in the province, according to the industry group's report, released Thursday.
When production, processing, and specialized equipment manufacturers are included, the maple syrup industry contributed $1.21 billion to the gross domestic product in 2025, the report said.
In total, the sector employs more than 10,000 full-time equivalent workers and generated $285 million in tax revenue, excluding municipal taxes and fees for the lease of public lands.
This figure does not include the sugar shacks that many Quebecers visit in the spring.
"Sugar shack operations are more akin to the restaurant industry," Turenne said.

The maple syrup producers' group used the recent election campaign to highlight the industry's importance as an employer and economic driver, and Goulet says the candidates were often surprised by the important role it played.
In some municipalities, "if you take away maple syrup production, you might as well shut down the villages," Goulet said.

articles.title: North Sea strikes could severely disrupt UK fuel supplies, union warns
articles.summary:
More than ⁠160 ​offshore rig workers plan walkout amid rising tensions between unions and oil companies

North Sea workers are preparing to strike at oil rigs across the ageing basin over…

blocks.text: North Sea workers are preparing to strike at oil rigs across the ageing basin over the coming weeks in a sign of growing tensions between trade unions and oil companies.
The Unite union said on ⁠Monday that more than ⁠160 ​offshore rig workers would take part ⁠in a 24-hour ​strike from Wednesday that could “severely disrupt” UK fuel supplies.
A 48-hour strike starting on Tuesday was already planned by workers at oil services company Wood Group contracted to Harbour Energy’s Britannia, Jasmine, Judy, Lomond and North Everest platforms.

Trade union leaders are scheduled to continue pay talks with the Apache energy company through the Acas mediation service on Wednesday. But Unite expects the 24-hour strike to go ahead at 6am that morning because, it says, the company has shown “no willingness” to resolve the dispute.

The strike will include workers employed at five Apache oil platforms linked to the Forties Pipeline System (FPS), which is responsible for about 30% of the UK’s oil production. Unite has claimed that a halt in production could lead to a sharp drop in pressure across the pipeline system and disrupt UK fuel supplies.
A spokesperson for Jim Ratcliffe’s Ineos, the owner of the Forties pipeline, did not respond to a request for comment.
North Sea oil companies have been on a collision course with trade unions in recent years as many cut investments in their UK assets, blaming the UK’s energy policies and tax regime.

The industrial action comes ahead of the budget on 28 October and an imminent decision on the fate of the controversial Jackdaw gas project, as the UK faces fresh concerns over its energy supplies this winter because of the global fuel crisis caused by the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine.

Texas-based Apache plans to end all its North Sea operations by the end of 2029, blaming the “onerous financial” impact of the government’s windfall tax, which means oil companies pay a total tax rate of 78% on their profits.

A spokesperson for Apache said it plans to use experienced contractors to continue production during the strike. It added that even if all five platforms were unable to operate, the company would not expect an impact on other oil companies using the Forties pipeline.

The company added: “Our offer provides a 4% pay increase for employees in the bargaining unit, whose earnings already place them among the highest earners in the UK and whose offshore rota averages 153 working days a year.”

Harbour Energy, the UK’s biggest producer of North Sea oil, has also blamed the UK’s tax regime for its decision to scale back investment in UK waters. It said late last year that it would cut 100 offshore jobs, having reduced its workforce by about 600 since 2023.

Wood Group said that only eight of the 150 employees contracted to the affected Harbour platforms took part in strike action earlier this month and that the action did not disrupt operations. A third 48-hour strike is planned for 3 November, according to Unite and trade union RMT.

articles.title: Minister says Mahmood’s migration policy will ‘prolong integration’
articles.summary:
In now-removed post, Miatta Fahnbulleh criticised home secretary’s proposal to extend qualifying period for settlement in UK

The energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, appears to have…

blocks.text: The energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, appears to have criticised Shabana Mahmood’s migration policy in a post on her constituency website, in which she suggested she had concerns that a longer settlement process could affect integration.

Fahnbulleh has since removed the critique, which appeared in a write-up of a community meeting in Peckham, her south London constituency, in September, saying it was not a true representation of her views.

In the original write-up of her comments at the town hall meeting, first highlighted by the Telegraph, Fahnbulleh was reported to have said: “If we continually prolong the time people have to wait for settlement, we can also prolong the process of building cohesion.” Her office said the remarks had been paraphrased, and would be rewritten to reflect a more accurate description of what she had told residents.

The government has proposed increasing the standard qualifying period for indefinite leave to remain from five years to 10, though it is likely to make concessions for some professions, including care workers.

The changes will also mean the pathway to permanent settlement for refugees is extended to up to 20 years, with reviews every 30 months. The government is yet to publish its long-anticipated final response to a consultation on the proposals – though the prime minister, Andy Burnham, has said he is committed to the bulk of the changes.

Tensions in the cabinet have already surfaced over the proposals. Last month the housing secretary, Angela Rayner, said in an interview that the proposed changes – if left unamended – would unfairly penalise care staff who had “moved their lives here to look after our loved ones”.

Fahnbulleh came to the UK as a child after fleeing the civil war in Liberia. Speaking to the Guardian’s Politics Weekly podcast last month, she admitted her family would have found Mahmood’s changes “tough”.
“I represent a constituency which is hugely diverse, where we’ve got first, second, third-generation immigrants, and how we navigate this landscape has been tough,” she added.
With Mahmood believed to be considering changing her plans, Fahnbulleh said she wanted the government to recognise migrants’ contributions.

“I think we ultimately need to get to an immigration system that has control … but actually then recognises the contribution that people have made. And if you’re in this country and you’re working – I say this as a refugee – and you’re doing your bit, and you’re part of your community, you’re working in our health service, then actually this should be a country that welcomes you,” she said.

“I wouldn’t be here if that wasn’t the way that we structured our immigration system. It has always been the case that this country is a welcoming country, and I’m sure it will continue to be that way.”

In her address to her Peckham constituents, Fahnbulleh said the debate had become “increasingly depressing and toxic”. She said there needed to be “a more compassionate immigration system. The asylum process is broken and needs reform. Ultimately, I want to see a system based on control and compassion, with a much stronger focus on integration.”

She continued: “Peckham is a good example of what can happen when communities are built deliberately, and people are given the opportunity to integrate and participate. If we continually prolong the time people have to wait for settlement, we can also prolong the process of building cohesion.

“We need to raise the level of the debate, challenge divisive political rhetoric and make the case for communities like the one we have in Peckham. That means talking about immigration with care, control and compassion.”

articles.title: 6 players to make worlds debut as Canadian women's hockey team looks to youth
articles.summary: The Canadian women's hockey team will take a young roster to the world championship in Denmark next month. It will be the first major tournament since the Canadians lost the Olympic final to the U.S.…

image.caption: Montreal Victoire forward Jessie Eldridge has played her way on to the Canadian women's national team's world championship roster. The Canadians will look to reclaim gold in Denmark, beginning on Nov. 6. (Jon Blacker/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: PWHL·New

The Canadian women's hockey team will take a young roster to the world championship in Denmark next month. It will be the first major tournament since the Canadians lost the Olympic final to the U.S. in February.
Shift comes after Canada lost to U.S. at Olympics, last year's world championship

When the Canadians arrive in Denmark in the coming weeks to try to reclaim the women's hockey world championship, it will be with a remarkably different roster than the one that lined up at the Olympics this past February.
That veteran-laden roster finished second to the Americans, after a hard-fought gold-medal game went into overtime.

Zoom further out, and you'll see a Canadian team that failed to beat the Americans over eight straight matchups. At times, the Canadians looked slower and less connected than the Americans, who embraced young talent over the last four years.
But if the roster for the first major tournament of a new Olympic quad is any indication, things are changing on Team Canada.
Six players will make their world championship debut next month in Denmark, which will host the world championship from Nov. 6 to 16.

items: Mix of young, veteran players invited to Canadian women's hockey team camp
Q&A: Nova Scotia woman named head coach of national women's hockey team

blocks.text: "There is a great sense of energy, hunger and determination within this group," head coach Kori Cheverie said in a statement. "We’re looking forward to building on that momentum as we prepare to compete in Denmark.”

The roster includes several players who have made a mark at the Under-18 level, including 18-year-old Rosalie Tremblay (University of Wisconsin), 18-year-old Hayley McDonald (Ohio State University), and 19-year-old Sara Manness (Clarkson University).
Nineteen-year-old defender Chloe Primerano is one of six college players who will suit up for Canada at the upcoming women's world championship. (Melissa Majchrzak/The Associated Press)

Three other collegiate players, 19-year-old Chloe Primerano (University of Minnesota), 20-year-old Caitlin Kraemer (University of Minnesota Duluth) and 23-year-old Ève Gascon (University of Minnesota Duluth) return for their second world championship.
Gascon has had a phenomenal start to her NCAA season, only allowing two goals in five games so far this season, while posting four shutouts.

Other players forced their way on to the team with stellar performances in the PWHL, including Ottawa Charge forwards Rebecca Leslie and Sarah Wozniewicz, PWHL Las Vegas defender Kendall Cooper, PWHL Hamilton defender Nicole Gosling, and Montreal Victoire forward Jessie Eldridge.

It will be Eldridge's first world-championship appearance since 2022, despite being one of the top offensive producers in the PWHL. Only three players have scored more goals than Eldridge since the league launched in 2024.

items: Hockey Canada clarifies that Nurse didn't decline invite, she's unable to attend camp
Canada to host U.S. ahead of women's hockey worlds

blocks.text: Leslie and Wozniewicz will make their world-championship debuts after helping lead the Ottawa Charge to the Walter Cup final. Leslie scored 14 goals in 30 regular-season games for Ottawa last season, tying Eldridge for second in the league, behind Minnesota's Kelly Pannek.
"This is a new landscape so the program needed to adapt to the new landscape," Canadian GM Danièle Sauvageau said last month, ahead of a training camp in Quebec City.

"The landscape is to look at who has success at the PWHL level, not only for a season but for the last [several seasons]. If you look closely, there are players in that category who have been successful. Now what we want to see is could they translate this success, this level of skill, this level of compete with the best-on-best at the international level. In order to know that, we need to see them and we need to obviously see what they can do among the group of the players that will be in Quebec City."
Several veterans to miss tournament

Only 13 members of the Olympic team were named to the roster. Several notable veterans will not be there, including captain Marie-Philip Poulin, who had major knee surgery in July. It's not yet clear when Poulin might be able to return to the ice.
Also absent is Vancouver Goldeneyes forward Sarah Nurse, who missed training camp with back issues, and Toronto Sceptres forward Blayre Turnbull, who is pregnant.
It's the first roster named by a new management group and coaching staff, led by Sauvageau and Cheverie.
Montreal Victoire head coach Kori Cheverie was named head coach of the Canadian women's national team this past summer. (Graham Hughes/The Canadian Press)
Cheverie's coaching staff will also include Caroline Ouellette (Montreal Victoire), Alison Domenico (University of Ottawa), and Kris Sparre (PWHL Hamilton).
Canada and the U.S. will play two exhibition games ahead of the world championship. The first will be on Oct. 28 in Windsor, Ont., followed by a game in Plymouth, Mich. on Oct. 30.
PWHL training camps are set to open on Nov. 18.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Karissa Donkin is a reporter with CBC Sports who covers the PWHL, women's hockey and lots more. You can reach her at karissa.donkin@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Marcoleta protests bid to field notary public as witness, Ombudsman sees 2027 case resolution
articles.summary: The camp of Senator Rodante Marcoleta flagged the prosecution"s attempt to present the attorney who notarized the deed of donations worth P75 million for Marcoleta"s campaign expenses.

blocks.text: Published October 20, 2026 1:28am

The camp of Senator Rodante Marcoleta flagged the prosecution’s attempt to present Cecil Federizo, the attorney who notarized the deed of donations worth P75 million in total for Marcoleta’s campaign expenses.

“They are expecting to obtain evidence from the witness to either prove that the deed of donation was not executed properly. This is a violation of presumption of innocence,” said Marcoleta’s counsel David Michael Gabriel, referring to the deed listing donations of P30 million dated Jan. 6, 2025, P25 million in January 8, 2025 and P20 million in January 9, 2025.
“If it's an attempt to impugn the deed of donation, then we have a problem,” he added.
The prosecution and the defense ultimately both agreed that it was Federizo who notarized the deeds of donation during the end of the last day of the prosecution’s evidence in chief last October 13.
The first day of the defense’s presentation of evidence is scheduled for Thursday, October 22.

Last Friday, Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla said he sees the Marcoleta case being resolved in a year because the prosecution was able to present its evidence within three months since they filed the case.
“When he asked for a bail hearing, we thought it best to present all our evidence immediately. And we rested our case already, which means it's his turn to present evidence,” Remulla said.

“We filed the case three months ago. If we took three months to present our case, he [Marcoleta] should have to do the same. We might be breaking records here, especially if the Sandiganbayan will really do its job in less than one year,” he added.
He said that the court taking 15 years to resolve a case, just like the pork barrel scam and fertilizer fund cases, should not be the norm.
“It is so important that we can break ground here, that this can be resolved within one year,” Remulla said.— BM, GMA News

articles.title: Petition urges McGill to allow convicted murderer on day parole back into law classes
articles.summary: Some students and alumni in McGill University's law faculty have signed a petition calling for the school to allow Jeffrey George Ewert, a convicted murderer on day parole, to return to campus.

image.caption: A petition signed by more than 100 students and alumni in McGill University's law faculty argues the exclusion of Jeffrey George Ewert from campus undermines his access to education and rehabilitation. (Kolya Hubacek-Guilbault/CBC)

blocks.text: Montreal·New
Some students and alumni in McGill University's law faculty have signed a petition calling for the school to allow Jeffrey George Ewert, a convicted murderer on day parole, to return to campus.
Law school grapples with fallout after paroled murderer excluded from campus
· CBC News
· Posted: Oct 19, 2026 1:16 PM EDT | Last Updated: 20 minutes ago
Now in his 60s, Ewert was convicted of second-degree murder and attempted murder for two attacks in B.C. in 1984.

He sexually assaulted and killed one woman and, less than six weeks later, beat and choked a 15-year-old so severely that she was paralyzed and disabled for life, according to a summary of his case in his parole board file.

Ewert is serving a life sentence and was granted day parole in 2025. While various clinical assessments ranked Ewert’s risk of reoffending as moderate to high, official parole documents say with close supervision at a halfway house and clinical follow-up, that risk “seems to fall more into the moderate risk category.”
Ewert is currently living in a halfway house. He declined an interview with CBC.

items: Convicted killer attending McGill law school divides students over safety, 2nd chances

blocks.text: He began attending law classes at McGill in August, but has not been seen on campus since early October, according to students. McGill's provost also confirmed that timeline in a letter Friday to students and alumni.
In a story published Friday, students told CBC News they were upset the university had not disclosed their peer’s violent history and some expressed feeling unsafe.
But the petition, signed by more than 100 students and alumni, argues the exclusion undermines Ewert's access to education and rehabilitation as an Indigenous man and a survivor of the Sixties Scoop.
Jeffrey George Ewert began attending law classes at McGill University in August. Some students told CBC they were upset his violent criminal past was not disclosed. (Name withheld/Instagram)
The petition, addressed to the university provost, the dean of the law faculty and the dean of students, acknowledges student safety concerns but says Ewert should not be excluded from campus.
"We are asking that Jeff be given the chance to do what the rest of us are doing, which is to attend class and learn," the petition says.
"A ban from the premises, with no conversation beforehand and no finding of misconduct, takes that chance away."
Debate among students
The CBC report has sparked heated debate among faculty, students and alumni.

An online discussion on Facebook features McGill law students on all sides of the controversy: some argue their peers should be more compassionate toward those convicted of a crime, while others say there should be more respect for students who feel unsafe.

"I can recognize the importance of reintegration, while also questioning how our university is handling the situation for students with such trauma," one person posted anonymously in the Facebook discussion.
"You never know what someone has been a victim to in their life and how that might impact their reaction, especially after having experienced such violence firsthand."
The administration, meanwhile, has tried to calm concerns among the student body.

items: Have a story worth digging into? Reach out to CBC Montreal Investigates

blocks.text: Tina Piper, the law faculty's dean, said in a letter to students that the university took "prompt action as soon as we became aware of this situation earlier this month."
Piper said she has been working with the administration on next steps.
"I want you to know that my highest priority is to ensure the safety and well-being of all members of our faculty," Piper said in the note, obtained by CBC.
"This situation is not unlike one you may encounter in your future legal career and now is a good time to practise how you want to be in the world."
In a separate email, McGill provost Angela Campbell also tried to reassure the university community.
She wrote that when information came to their attention about a situation that could "compromise a safe learning environment," the university took measured, decisive action.
Convicted killer attending McGill law school divides students over safety, 2nd chances
Ewert 'an example of rehabilitation,' lawyer says
Ewert’s lawyer, Nora Demnati, said his admission to McGill’s law program was a continuation of two decades of legal advocacy while he was in prison.
Ewert heads the Canadian Prisoners’ Labour Confederation, a group that advocates for labour rights for inmates.
She said the situation has “put tremendous stress on someone who’s like, honestly, an example of rehabilitation,” said Demnati.
While Demnati said she understands the concerns of some students, she believes they come from an “uninformed” reading of the parole decisions.
“Parole is based on progress and work and it’s on merit," said Demnati in an interview with CBC last week.

When Ewert’s parole was extended in June, some of his conditions included not to enter a drinking establishment, to immediately report all sexual and non-sexual relationships with women and to allow his case management team access to all his telecommunication activity.

That latter condition was added by the parole board because Ewert had been viewing women’s profiles on social media, starting discussions with them and exploring a dating site without notifying his case management team.
He was reprimanded by the parole board in 2025 after he had contacted and collected the phone numbers of multiple women.
As parolees are adjusting to life outside prison, Demnati said it’s normal for there to be occasional breaches.
“People on parole have breaches a lot of the time,” she said. “It does not lead necessarily to an increase in the risk and it does not lead to a conclusion that the risk cannot be managed anymore.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Benjamin Shingler is an investigative reporter based in Montreal. He previously worked at The Canadian Press, CTV and the New Brunswick Telegraph-Journal. You can email story ideas or tips to montrealinvestigates@cbc.ca, or reach out on Signal at @bshingler.67

articles.title: Journalists forced to flee homes after Tommy Robinson shared images of where they lived online, court told
articles.summary:
Far-right activist is charged with two counts of harassment causing fear of violence to two MailOnline reporters

Journalists and their family members had to flee their homes after “bullyboy,…

blocks.text: Journalists and their family members had to flee their homes after “bullyboy, intimidatory tactics” were deployed by the far-right activist known as Tommy Robinson, a court has been told as his harassment trial got under way.

Robinson, 42, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, was alleged to have targeted journalists from the Daily Mail and Mail Online by circulating images of their homes to millions of online followers and in effect encouraging them to join in making threats.
He is charged with two counts of harassment causing fear of violence to two MailOnline journalists, Andrew Young and Jacob Dirnhuber in 2024, which Robinson denies.

Dirnhuber, a senior editor at the Mail, and his partner had to leave their home, while Young and his family were provided with a close protection officer after the alleged campaign of intimidation by Robinson.

Robinson, a former member of the British National Party (BNP) and co-founder of the English Defence League (EDL), is accused of harassment causing fear of violence through X posts and direct messages. He is also alleged to have made a telephone call on 5 August 2024 in which he is accused of telling Young he would visit his house, saying: “I’m coming to get you.”

Opening the case for the prosecution on Monday at Southwark Crown Court, barrister Ben Holt told the jury Robinson could have chosen to complain to a press regulator after the Mail reported on his alleged role as an “influencer” encouraging the violence that broke out after the Southport murders in July 2024.

The paper’s coverage included photos of Robinson reclining on a sunlounger, a phone in hand, while on holiday in Cyprus, where a team from the Daily Mail had located him. Members of the jury were shown an image of a front page which included a photo of Robinson and the headline: “Stoking Race Riots from his Sunbed.”
“This trial is about the defendant’s reaction to this, what he perceived to be, unnecessary intrusion into his holiday,” said Holt.

“On social media, to millions of followers, he circulated images of their homes. His supporters, followers, got involved, threatening the journalists. Understandably, you might agree, they were scared, in some circumstances being forced to leave their homes.

“That is what this trial is actually about. The prosecution say this defendant, using bullyboy, intimidatory tactics, threatened the journalists. He sent photographers to their home addresses. He put pictures, albeit redacted, of them out on his timeline on X for the enjoyment and appreciation of his followers.
Holt took the jury through Robinson’s reaction on X to the Mail’s coverage, which was said to have changed in tone from being “reasonable” and “concerned” to “retaliatory”.
Holt said that it was was inevitable “and would have been known” by Robinson that his online followers and supporters “would pick up the baton and attack” those he was talking about.

Examples given included tweets from an X account using the name The Secret SpAd, which posted the home address of Young while the journalist was still in Cyprus. It was posted with the comment: ”Please be sure to congratulate him.”

When Young returned home from Cyprus on 6 August, his wife and daughters told him that a man in a grey Audi had parked outside their home. The man was confronted by the journalist’s daughter but ignored her, and a report was made to police. A further report was made of a man sitting under a tree, pointing his camera at the house.
Holt told the court: “Mr Young was concerned. His main concern was that while (Robinson) himself might not harm him, one of his many supporters online may seek revenge on him or his family.”

The court heard that a third journalist who was involved the mail’s coverage, George Odling, also felt the need to leave his family home after becoming concerned with the publicity surrounding his colleagues.

Ted Verity, the editor-in-chief of the newspaper, provided evidence to police of a voicemail he received from an individual who identified himself as Tommy Robinson, who allegedly told him: “I’ve already located every fucking one of you.”
A video posted by Robinson’s X account was also played to the court, in which he accused the Mail of having “doxxed” his family and children.

In the video, he sad: “You broke up my family holiday. Is it fair that I do that to you? You know I know the locations to where you are. To any other journalist, I will find you. So please, think: is it right?”
The trial was adjourned until Tuesday morning.

articles.title: Ferocious criticism from all sides underlines Macron’s isolation
articles.summary: French president has compounded impression of arrogance with strategic errors – and consequences could be profound

blocks.text: The near-universal chorus of condemnation that greeted Emmanuel Macron’s address to the nation on Sunday, after one of the most violent days of rioting and looting in France’s recent history, was a stark reflection of just how weakened he now is.

Speaking from his office at the Élysée Palace, the president delivered an eight-minute speech expressing “anger and shame” after a weekend in which a town hall was set ablaze, 2,000-plus shops were looted, 2,300 people were arrested and 1,000 police injured.

A month-long protest by high school pupils over crumbling and crowded classrooms converged with broader frustrations over soaring living costs, rapidly widening inequality and falling public spending, bringing together students, teachers, trade unionists and a resurrected gilets jaunes movement.

Those largely peaceful protests were swiftly hijacked by masked groups who torched vehicles, ransacked businesses and severely damaged public infrastructure, including setting fire to Limoges’ city hall and invading that of Marseille.

Macron acknowledged the “deep anxiety” of young people but offered no concrete policy initiatives, no cabinet reshuffle and no new public spending, merely telling his prime minister to organise consultations and asking opposition politicians to take a stand.

The response, across the political spectrum, was damning. The Greens’ leader, Marine Tondelier, said that rather than “even beginning to make any kind of mea culpa”, Macron was “summoning us to the PM’s office like pupils to the blackboard”.

On the far right, the National Rally’s Jordan Bardella called the speech “lamentable” and said Macron had “nothing left to say” to the French. The party’s figurehead, Marine Le Pen, said the country was “caught in a vice between violence and impotence”.

The centre-right’s Bruno Retailleau said Macron was “totally overwhelmed”, while on the radical left, Jean-Luc Mélenchon accused the president of relying on “inaction and police brutality” in doomed hopes that the protests would simply fizzle out.

Perhaps most damagingly, even Macron’s former prime minister Édouard Philippe said he would have preferred “decisions and initiatives that might lead to a return to order and the restoration of state authority … Our country needs to be governed.”

Criticism is to be expected from rivals positioning themselves six months before a presidential election to choose Macron’s successor. But its sheer ferocity underlines his isolation, the disdain in which he is held, and the anger he inspires.

It is a structural trap that he has largely set for himself. Macron came to power in 2017 as a “Jupiterian” president – a deliberate strategy aimed at elevating the head of state above daily politics, projecting distant authority and technocratic brilliance.

But over nine years in the Élysée, that high-handed style – partly born, his critics say, of Macron’s complete lack of basic political experience as an elected official in a town hall or as a constituency MP – has morphed into perceived arrogance and detachment.

It has been compounded by catastrophic strategic errors, and France’s spiralling economic problems. Macron lost a functional parliamentary majority by refusing to meaningfully campaign between the presidential and legislative elections of 2022.

Two years later he dissolved the national assembly. That gamble backfired spectacularly, with voters returning an even more deadlocked parliament split between a divided left, a much-diminished centrist bloc and Le Pen’s far right.

Without a working majority, the government repeatedly resorted to controversial constitutional manoeuvres to force through laws without a parliamentary vote, laying it – and Macron – open to further accusations of democratic illegitimacy.

Compounding that institutional deadlock is a looming fiscal crisis. In decades gone by, French presidents facing mass protests on the streets could in effect buy a degree of social tranquility with targeted spending packages or public sector concessions.

But France’s national debt, at 119% of GDP, is at its highest level since 1946. Its budget deficit, at 5.1%, is also among the highest in the EU. There is just no money in the bank to ease the cost of living squeeze that brought 550,000 people on to the streets on Saturday.

The markets are worried: France’s borrowing costs are higher than Greece’s. And with few fiscal options, the government’s clearest response – in time-honoured French tradition – has been teargas and baton charges, sometimes against schoolchildren, further aggravating tensions.

The consequences for the presidential election could be profound. The centrist coalition built around Macron’s brand has all but collapsed. If the protests and violence persist, the main beneficiary will be the law-and-order champions of the far right.

Jean-Baptiste Moreau, an influential former MP from Macron’s party with whom the largely lame-duck president still occasionally speaks, reportedly went so far this weekend as to suggest he should resign and call early presidential elections.
“Macron still thinks he can change things,” he told Le Monde. “But at the moment, Marine Le Pen is on a direct path to the Élysée Palace.”

articles.title: Warning signs over threats to Australian politicians were rising before MP hit by car
articles.summary: The apparent attack on MP Helen Haines suggests the worst fears of politicians and public figures appear to have been realised.

blocks.text: As increasingly frequent acts of violence against politicians have shocked the globe in recent years, Australia has watched on with a contradictory feeling: that attacks like that could not happen here, and that it was only a matter of time until they did.

Australians will tell you this is a largely peaceful society with a comparatively civil public discourse. Violence targeting politicians has been rare, the bungled assassination of Labor leader Arthur Calwell in 1966 now a distant and fleeting memory.
But MPs and public figures – backed by experts – have been warning of a volcano of threats against them as social cohesion cracks, polarisation intensifies and the tone of debate grows hotter.
And on Monday, their worst fears appear to have been realised.
Independent MP Helen Haines was struck by a car and severely injured outside her office in the regional Victorian town of Wangaratta.
Police say a 43-year-old man was arrested at the scene, and a knife seized, but they have not said Haines was hit deliberately.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, however, swiftly described the incident as an apparent attack.

He was briefed by federal police – whose counter terror squad is helping state officers investigate – and told the national broadcaster: "This wasn't an accident. There was a deliberate act, it would appear."
Though he stressed no motive had been confirmed, Albanese earlier got emotional as he talked about the growing fear amongst MPs that they would end up targets.

Earlier this year Albanese himself was evacuated from his official residence over a bomb threat. As of August, about 20 cases in which people were accused of making violent threats against him were winding their way through courts around the country.

In recent years, politicians here have been mailed bullets. Female MPs – and in some cases their children – have been threatened with sexual violence. A Jewish MP's office has been firebombed, a Sydney mayor's car has been torched and countless other politicians have had their workplaces vandalised.

Just last week Small Business Minister Anne Aly said she had received a wave of death threats after a politician from the opposition said she should be "shamed and stoned in the square" over a tax policy.
According to government statistics, there were 1,067 reports of "harassing and threatening behaviour" against "high office holders" in the year to June: an increase on last year.
"We tend to bury our head in the sand and say, 'Not here', but this has been happening now for well over a decade," Josh Roose, a Deakin University Professor on violent extremism, tells the BBC.

Socioeconomic strain, growing mental health problems in the community, "grifters" who benefit politically or financially from whipping up further discontent, and a "carcinogenic" online environment are drivers of the trend, he says, which has dramatically escalated since the pandemic.
But the political class must also take responsibility for their role, he adds.

"We've seen a willingness to cross previously sacred terrain - you know, not targeting individuals, not targeting their families - but we now see that this is part and parcel of Australian political life.
"This is occurring at both ends of the political spectrum."
And experts like him warn it is not just politicians who are vulnerable: it is members of the media, academics, court officials and other public figures too.
Mike Burgess, the head of Australia's spy agency, has warned for years that the spectre of political violence is looming in Australia.

"Just as climate change increases the likelihood of extreme weather but does not forecast specific storms, politically motivated violence, including acts of terrorism, is more likely even though we cannot predict a specific attack," he said in his annual threat assessment for 2026.
And the Federal Police have said it is not just ideology motivating cases in recent times. "Grievance" is radicalising people.
"They're feeling distanced, they're feeling alone, they're looking for something to attach to, to give them meaning and purpose," Commissioner Krissy Barrett told the ABC earlier this month.

There have been frustrated rumblings in Canberra from some MPs who say security arrangements have not changed with the climate and – if a political motivation for this incident is confirmed – one of the greatest tenets of the nation's political culture could now be at risk.
It is not abnormal for you to run into your local member at the shops, or chat to them at the footy, and many open up their offices for constituents who want to raise concerns or share ideas.
Haines is particularly renowned and respected for that, Albanese said on Monday night.
"Here in Australia, it is a good thing that politicians are able to go about their community and engage with people," he said.

"I don't want to see a political system in which you can't have conversations with people at the supermarket, in the street, at street meetings, public forums – that's an important part of our democracy."

articles.title: Ex-OpenAI worker accused of planting device had Saudi support says court filing
articles.summary: The Saudi government did not immediately respond to BBC requests for comment.

blocks.text: A Saudi national charged with secretly planting a recording device in one of OpenAI's meeting rooms has been accused of having "considerable support" from the Saudi government, according to a court filing, external in California.

US prosecutors claimed Abdulrahman Alfozan, who worked for the AI firm, was in "frequent communication... with a member of the Saudi royal family", and say a member of the country's military paid for a one-way flight to Saudi Arabia for his wife and son after his arrest.
It was argued the 35-year-old engineer therefore posed a flight risk and should be detained, pending trial.
The Saudi government did not immediately respond to BBC requests for comment.
Alfozan had worked at OpenAI for around a year before he allegedly made his attempt to plant an audio recorder.
The AI company discovered the device, which was plugged into the back of a TV in a conference meeting room and covered up with toilet paper, on 30 September.
A camera was placed in the room and on 5 October, Alfozan was filmed entering and appearing to look behind the television where the audio recorder had been inserted.
He was arrested by the FBI on 9 October and his contract with OpenAI was terminated.

The court filing claimed the suspect's alleged conduct could pose "a danger to the national security of the United States", because executives from the tech firm met with government officials in the room during the days the device was believed to have been installed.
It said Alfozan's arrest came three days before he was scheduled to fly from San Francisco to Riyadh on a one-way itinerary with his wife and son.

Following the arrest, the document claims the defendant's wife told FBI agents who interviewed her that "her US visa was expiring" and so she and her son were "permanently moving back to Saudi Arabia", and her husband intended to do the same.

On 10 October, the day after Alfozan was arrested, his wife and son flew from San Francisco to Doha, Qatar. They travelled on a one-way business class ticket booked and paid for by a Saudi military official.
"Ultimately, the defendant has little incentive to remain in the United States to see this case through," the prosecutors argued.
The FBI investigation is ongoing.
Alfozan is scheduled to ‌appear ⁠in federal court in San Francisco later on Monday. If convicted, he faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $250,000 (£188,000) fine.

articles.title: Houthi missile strike on Yemen camp kills 50 security recruits, local authorities say
articles.summary: Three missiles hit a camp in government-controlled Shabwa province that officials say was being used as a training centre for new recruits.

blocks.text: More than 50 security personnel have been killed and 200 injured in a Houthi missile strike on a camp in Yemen's central province of Shabwa, local authorities say.

A spokesman for the Saudi-backed Yemeni armed forces said the Iran-backed group launched three ballistic missiles at al-Alam camp near Ataq city, which was being used as a training centre for recruits to the security forces and police.
The head of Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council, Rashad al-Alimi, condemned what he called the "criminal attack" and promised a "firm response".
The Houthis' military spokesman said they had targeted "Saudi enemy concentrations".
Yemen's devastating civil war has flared up in recent months.
At the start of October, pro-government forces launched a major offensive that aims to retake territory in western Yemen that is controlled by the Houthis.

With air support from a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states, they managed to regain control of territory on the Red Sea coast that overlooks the strategically important Bab al-Mandab Strait, which the Houthis captured in a surprise assault in September.
However, fierce fighting is continuing there, as well as around the besieged government-controlled city of Taiz, and to the north in Marib and al-Jawf provinces.
The Houthis have also responded to the Saudi air strikes by launching missiles and drones at airports, energy facilities and military bases in neighbouring Saudi Arabia.
Monday's attack in Shabwa is one of the deadliest reported since the start of the escalation.

Shabwa province's media office said in a statement that ballistic missiles struck the Martyr Ahmed al-Sulaimani Training Centre, where recruits from several provinces were undergoing training to be members of the internal security forces. According to a preliminary assessment, 53 were killed and more than 200 injured, it added.
A video posted on social media appeared to show several bodies scattered across the ground.

Shabwa's deputy governor, Fahad al-Khalifi, told AFP news agency that hospitals in the province were overwhelmed and had been forced to transfer the most seriously wounded to neighbouring Hadramout and Aden, where the government is based. Some of them were in a critical condition, he said.
Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani said the attack constituted a war crime because the internal security forces training centre was not a military target.

He also accused the Houthis of "attempting to fabricate a false media victory, boost the morale of its collapsing elements, and cover up the defeats and setbacks it is suffering across various combat axes".
The Houthis' military spokesman, Yahya Sarea, said in a statement that the missiles targeted a gathering of "Saudi enemy" forces at al-Alam camp, which he said was run by Saudi officers.
There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities.

In a separate development, Houthi-run media reported that a Saudi air strike on a home in the Sahar district of the Houthi-controlled northern province of Saada on Sunday killed at least 10 people and injured 23 others, many of them women and children.
According to the Houthi-run health ministry in north-western Yemen, a total of 141 people had been killed in Saudi strikes over the past seven weeks.
The government's health ministry, meanwhile, said last week that at least 1,282 people had been killed in the conflict across Yemen since 6 August.
In Saudi Arabia, at least 19 people have been killed in Houthi attacks targeting the kingdom's airports since the beginning of October.

Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.

A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

articles.title: Obama blasts federal probe of congresswoman Ilhan Omar as 'so appalling'
articles.summary: Obama says federal agents' search of the Democrat's home was an effort to intimidate a Trump critic.

blocks.text: Barack Obama has said congresswoman Ilhan Omar is under federal criminal investigation simply because she's an outspoken critic of the President Donald Trump.

"The full weight of the federal government is being brought down on a law-abiding elected official because she has dared to criticize the president," the former US president wrote on X, calling the probe "so appalling".
The White House defended the inquiry, saying the justice department was "focused on restoring law and order".

Last week, homeland security agents searched the Minnesota Democrat's Washington DC home as part of an investigation into her immigration status. Born in Somalia, Omar moved to the US with her family as a child.
US media outlets have reported that the probe is tied to her American citizenship and whether she lied about her age when she arrived in the US in 1995.
Questions have been raised about whether the age listed on Omar's citizenship application differed from her actual birth date.
Obama said in his X post on Sunday that her father became a naturalised citizen when she was 17, and not yet legally an adult, which then gave her citizenship.

"Now the Administration is actively trying to deport Congresswoman Omar, seemingly based solely on the unsubstantiated theory that she was actually 18 when her father was naturalized, and therefore is not a citizen," he wrote.
"If this becomes the new normal," he added, "there's no reason to believe it will stop with her - or that future presidents, in either party, won't do the same."

According to the US Citizenship and Immigration Services, a child born outside of the US automatically becomes a citizen when he or she has at least one parent who is a citizen by birth or naturalisation, or he or she is under the age of 18, and is a lawful permanent resident living in the custody of a citizen parent.
White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis denied the investigation was politically motivated.
"Unlike Joe Biden, President Trump has not weaponized the Department of Justice against his political foes," she said in an emailed statement to the BBC.
"The Department is focused on restoring law and order and keeping Americans safe."
Trump has often argued that federal criminal investigations against him as he campaigned for re-election were politically motivated.

The investigation into Omar could lead to the justice department seeking to "denaturalise" her, or revoke her citizenship. It would have to prove there were material lies in the naturalisation process.
In 2023, Republicans removed Omar from the House Foreign Affairs Committee for comments and tweets she made about Israel, which drew bipartisan criticism.
Omar has said that Trump has targeted her for years with "baseless lies and smear campaigns" and called the investigation "the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation".
But Trump has said the investigation had "nothing to do" with him, while describing Omar as a "terrible person" and a "complainer".
Federal agents reportedly seized her phone, computers, notebooks and passport in the raid a week ago.

Her lawyers have demanded the government return her belongings, CBS News, the BBC's US partner, has reported, arguing in a letter sent on Friday that the seizure of property had violated restrictions put in place by a judge to protect her work as a federal lawmaker.

The lawyers also alleged agents did not duly notify Omar or the House of Representatives general counsel that a search would be taking place and kept her from contacting her attorney for more than an hour, according to CBS.

Democrats characterised the raid as the president attempting to interfere with the legislative branch of government. Republicans, meanwhile, have said Omar should be treated the same as anyone else under the law.

When Obama first ran for president, and throughout his two terms in the White House, Trump repeatedly raised questions about his citizenship, asserting he was not born on American soil and was disqualified from serving in office. Obama released two records proving he had been born in Hawaii.
Obama did not mention that history in his X post on Sunday.
